editorialDecl.p: New English translation produced by the Falsafa project (Thothica) using an in-house agentic AI translation system, rendered from the Perseus source edition and reviewed by the project. Contributed to provide a translation for a work that previously had no English translation in the corpus.

div.p: Though I am very far from wishing to deliver the kind of prefatory discourse that is customarily attached to historical works, I am nonetheless compelled to say something about myself at the outset. I shall not dwell upon my own praises, which I know strike listeners as wearisome, nor have I resolved to cast slanders upon rival historians, as Anaximenes and Theopompus did in the prefaces to their histories; rather, I shall set forth the reasonings I employed when I first set my hand to this undertaking, and render an account of the sources from which I gained my knowledge of the matters to be related. 1.2. For I have become convinced that those who would leave to posterity memorials of their own minds—memorials that will not perish from time together with their bodies—must above all, if they are writers of history (in which we hold truth to be enshrined, that source of prudence and wisdom), first choose subjects that are noble and magnificent and that bring great benefit to their readers; and next prepare with great care and diligence the resources suited to the writing of that subject. 1.3. For those who lay the foundations of historical works upon matters that are inglorious, or base, or unworthy of any serious effort—whether from a craving to advance into public notice and win a name of any sort whatever, or from a wish to display the abundance of their literary power—are neither envied by posterity for their knowledge nor praised for their ability; they leave behind in those who take up their histories only the opinion that their own lives were of the same kind as the writings they published. For men quite reasonably hold that a man's discourses are images of his soul. 1.4. Yet those who choose the finest subjects, but compose them carelessly and slackly out of whatever reports happen to come to hand, win no praise for their choice; for we do not think it fitting that histories recording famous cities and men who have held positions of power should be improvised or thrown together negligently. 1.5. Believing, then, that these are necessary and primary considerations for historians, and having taken great care over both, I have been unwilling either to pass over the discussion of them or to assign it to any place more fitting than the preface of my work. 2.1. That the subject I have chosen is a noble one, magnificent, and useful to many, I do not think will require many words to demonstrate—at least to those not wholly unacquainted with universal history. For if a man should turn his mind to the dominions of cities and nations handed down to us from the past, and then, examining each separately and comparing them one with another, should wish to determine which of them acquired the greatest empire and displayed the most brilliant achievements both in peace and in war, he will see that the dominion of the Romans has far surpassed all those recorded before it—not only in the magnitude of its rule and the splendour of its achievements, which as yet no account has fittingly adorned, but also in the length of time during which it has endured down to our own age. 2.2. For the empire of the Assyrians, ancient as it was and reaching back into mythical times, held sway over only a small part of Asia. The Median empire, having overthrown that of the Assyrians and embraced a wider dominion, did not endure for long, but was dissolved in the fourth generation. The Persians, who vanquished the Medes, in the end gained control of almost all of Asia; but when they attacked the nations of Europe as well, they subdued no great number of them, and they remained in power for not much more than two hundred years. 2.3. The Macedonian power, having overthrown the strength of the Persians, surpassed all empires before it in the magnitude of its rule; yet even this did not flourish for long, but after the death of Alexander began to decline. For, torn apart among many leaders immediately after the Successors, and after them retaining its strength as far as the second or third generation, it grew feeble of itself, and in the end was destroyed by the Romans. 2.4. And not even this empire made the whole earth and sea subject to it; for it gained control neither of Libya, save the part near Egypt, which is of no great extent, nor did it subdue the whole of Europe, but advanced in its northern parts only as far as Thrace, and in its western descended only as far as the Adriatic Sea. 3.1. The most illustrious of the earlier dominions, then, which we have received from history, attained such a height of power and strength only to be destroyed. As for the Greek powers, it is not fitting to set them beside these for comparison, since they attained neither so great a magnitude of empire nor so long a span of pre-eminence as those did. 3.2. The Athenians, for their part, ruled only the seaboard, and that for sixty-eight years, and not even all of it, but only the part within the Euxine Sea and the Pamphylian gulf, in the time when their command of the sea was at its height. The Lacedaemonians, holding the mastery of the Peloponnese and the rest of Greece, extended their rule as far as Macedonia, but were brought to a halt by the Thebans, having held their dominion not even a full thirty years. 3.3. But the city of Rome rules over all the earth that is not inaccessible but inhabited by men, and holds sway over the whole sea—not only that within the Pillars of Heracles, but also the Ocean, so far as it can be sailed—being the first and only city of all those recorded from the beginning of time to make the rising and the setting of the sun the boundaries of its dominion. Nor has its span of power been brief, but greater than that of any other city or kingdom whatsoever. 3.4. For from the very beginning, immediately after its founding, it began to draw to itself the neighbouring peoples, who were many and warlike, and to advance ever onward, subjugating all that stood against it. These events now stand at seven hundred and forty-five years, down to the consulship of Claudius Nero (his second) and Calpurnius Piso, who were appointed in the third year of the hundred and ninety-third Olympiad. And from the time when Rome gained control of all Italy and took heart to advance to the empire of all mankind—expelling from the sea the Carthaginians, who possessed the greatest naval power, and bringing under its hand Macedonia, which 3.5. until then had seemed to be the mightiest power upon land—having no longer any rival, whether barbarian race or Greek nation, it has now continued for the seventh generation, the one of my own day, ruling over every region; and there is scarcely a nation, one may say, that disputes with it over the common dominion or refuses to be ruled by it. 3.6. But indeed, that I have neither chosen the meanest of subjects, as I said, nor resolved to occupy myself with trifling and obscure deeds, but write of the most renowned of cities and of achievements than which no man could point to others more brilliant—of this I do not know that I need say more. 4.1. But that it was not without reason and prudent forethought that I turned to the ancient history of this city, but had sound grounds to give for my choice, I wish to say a few words in advance, lest some of those who find fault with everything should rebuke me—having heard nothing as yet of what is to be set forth—on the ground that, while the city that has become renowned in our day took its first beginnings from obscure and quite humble origins, unworthy of historical record, and reached distinction and fame only a few generations ago, from the time when it overthrew the Macedonian powers and brought the Phoenician wars to a successful close, I, who might have taken some one of its illustrious subjects, have inclined instead toward an antiquity that has nothing distinguished about it. 4.2. For the ancient history of the city of Rome is still all but unknown among the Greeks; and certain opinions, not true but taking their origin from chance reports, have deceived the many—as though Rome owed its founding to certain homeless wanderers and barbarians, and these not even free men, and as though it had not advanced in time to the empire of all mankind through piety and justice and every other virtue, but through some chance and an unjust fortune that bestows at random the greatest of goods upon the least deserving. And the more malicious are accustomed to accuse Fortune openly, on the ground that she provides the goods of the Greeks to barbarians, the basest of men. 4.3. And why need I speak of the rest, when even some of the historians have ventured to write these things and leave them behind in their histories—gratifying barbarian kings who hated our dominion, kings to whom they were themselves enslaved and whose pleasures they continually served, by composing histories that were neither just nor true? 5.1. Resolving, then, to remove these mistaken notions, as I said, from the minds of the many, and to set up the true ones in their place, I shall set forth in this work, concerning the founders of the city—who they were, at what several times each group came together, and by what fortunes they were driven to abandon the homes of their fathers. And through it I undertake to show that they were Greeks, and that they came together from no insignificant or 5.2. mean nations. As for the deeds they displayed immediately after the founding, and the practices through which their descendants advanced to so great a dominion, I shall recount them, beginning with the record that follows upon this one, omitting nothing worthy of history so far as lies within my power—so that those who have learned the truth may be moved to feel toward this city what is fitting, unless they are altogether savage and hostile in their disposition toward it; that they may neither chafe at the subjection which has come about as was natural (for it is a law of Nature common to all, which no time shall abolish, that the stronger shall always rule the weaker), nor accuse Fortune of having bestowed so great a dominion, and for so long a time, gratis upon a city unworthy of it— 5.3. learning, that is, from history that Rome brought forth countless virtues in her men from the very first, immediately after the founding; men more pious, more just, more temperate throughout their whole lives, and braver in the contests of war, than any city ever produced, whether Greek or barbarian—if only the odium of envy be kept far from my words; for there is something of that kind even in the promise of marvels and wonders. 5.4. But all those men together, who invested the city with so great a magnitude of dominion, are unknown among the Greeks, having met with no historian of note; for no accurate history of them in the Greek tongue has appeared down to our own times, save only summary epitomes, very brief. 6.1. The first to touch upon Roman antiquity, so far as I myself am aware, was Hieronymus of Cardia, in his work on the Successors; next, Timaeus of Sicily related the ancient portion of the history in his general work, while he assigned the wars against Pyrrhus of Epirus to a separate treatise. Together with these, Antigonus and Polybius and Silenus and countless others have addressed themselves to the same matters, though not all alike—each of them having recorded only a few things, and these not even carefully studied, but put together from chance reports. 6.2. Histories similar to these, and in no way different, have also been published by such of the Romans as wrote of the ancient achievements of the city in the Greek tongue; the oldest of these are Quintus Fabius and Lucius Cincius, both of whom flourished during the Phoenician wars. Each of these men recorded accurately, from his own experience, the events in which he himself took part, but ran over only summarily the ancient matters that occurred after the founding of the city. 6.3. For these reasons, then, it seemed good to me not to pass over a noble history that had been left unrecorded by my predecessors—a history from which, if it be accurately written, the best and most just of results will follow: for those good men who have fulfilled their allotted portion, to win everlasting glory and to be praised by posterity, which makes mortal nature like unto the divine and keeps men's deeds from dying together with their bodies; 6.4. and for the descendants of those godlike men, both those now living and those who shall come hereafter, to choose not the most pleasant and easiest of lives, but the most noble and ambitious, reflecting that those who have received from their lineage fine first beginnings ought to think greatly of themselves and to practise nothing unworthy of their forefathers. 6.5. As for myself—who have inclined to this undertaking not for the sake of flattery, but out of regard for truth and justice, at which all history must aim—my purpose is, first, to display the disposition of my own mind, that it is well-disposed toward all good men and lovers of noble and great deeds; and next, to render to the city such thank-offerings as lay within my power, mindful of the education and the other blessings I enjoyed during my sojourn in it. 7.1. Now that I have given my account of the choice I have made, I wish to say something further about the sources I used when I was about to set my hand to the writing. For perhaps those who have read Hieronymus, or Timaeus, or Polybius, or some other of the historians of whom I spoke a little earlier as having handled their writing carelessly, finding that much of what I write is not to be found set down in those authors, will suppose that I am inventing, and will demand to learn whence this knowledge has come to me. So that no such opinion of me may take hold of anyone, it is better to state in advance the discourses and 7.2. records from which I started. I sailed to Italy at the very time when the civil war was brought to an end by Augustus Caesar, in the middle of the hundred and eighty-seventh Olympiad; and having since that time spent in Rome the two-and-twenty years down to the present, learning the Roman tongue and acquiring a knowledge of the native writings, throughout all this period I continued to occupy myself with whatever bore upon this undertaking. 7.3. Some things I received by instruction from the most learned men with whom I came into conversation; others I gathered out of the histories written by those Romans who are commended by their own countrymen—Porcius Cato, Fabius Maximus, Valerius of Antium, Licinius Macer, the Aelii and Gellii and Calpurnii, and many other men of note besides these. Setting out from those works (which resemble the Greek chronicles), I then undertook the writing. 7.4. So much, then, I have discussed concerning myself. It remains for me to say something further about the history itself: within what limits of time I confine it, what matters I make the subject of my narrative, and what form I give to the work. 8.1. I begin my history, then, with the most ancient legends, which the historians before me passed over as being difficult to discover without great labour; 8.2. and I bring my narrative down to the beginning of the First Phoenician War, which fell in the third year of the hundred and twenty-eighth Olympiad. I recount all the foreign wars the city waged in those times, and all the civil dissensions in which it was embroiled, from what causes they arose and by what means and arguments they were composed. I go through all the forms of government it employed, both under the kings and after the overthrow of the monarchs, and what the character of each of them was. I describe its noblest customs and most notable laws, and in sum I set forth the whole ancient life of the city. 8.3. As for the form I give the work, it is neither such as those who have recorded wars alone have given to their histories, nor such as those who have treated of constitutions by themselves, nor like the chronicles published by those who have dealt with the Attic annals—for these are uniform in kind and soon become tedious to their hearers. Rather, it is a form blended of every kind—the agonistic, the speculative, and the pleasing—so that it may appear satisfactory both to those who occupy themselves with political discourse, and to those who have devoted themselves to philosophical inquiry, and to any who may require an untroubled recreation in historical reading. 8.4. Such, then, are the matters of which my history will treat, and such the form it will assume. Its author is Dionysius of Halicarnassus, son of Alexander. And I begin from this point. 9.1. The city that is mistress of all the earth and sea, which the Romans now inhabit, is said to have been held, in the most ancient times recorded, by barbarian Sicels, a native people; what came before them—whether the land was held by others or was uninhabited—no one can say with certainty. In later time the Aborigines took possession of it, having wrested it from its holders in a long war. 9.2. These had formerly dwelt in the mountains, without walls, in scattered villages; but when the Pelasgians and certain others of the Greeks mingled with them and joined in their war against their neighbours, they drove out the Sicel race from the land, surrounded themselves with many cities, and brought into subjection to themselves all the territory bounded by two rivers, the Liris and the Tiber. These rivers take the beginning of their course from the foothills of the Apennine mountains, by which all Italy is cleft in two along its length; and parting from one another at their mouths by some eight hundred stades, they pour forth into the Tyrrhenian Sea—the Tiber emptying from the northern parts near the city of Ostia, and the Liris from the southern region, passing by Minturnae. 9.3. Both of these are colonies of the Romans. And the same people continued to dwell in the same region, never again driven out by others, though called by two successive changes of name: down to the Trojan War still preserving the ancient appellation of the Aborigines, but in the reign of King Latinus, who held power during the war of Ilium, beginning to be called Latins. 9.4. And when Romulus founded the city named after himself, sixteen generations after the Trojan War, they took the name they now bear, and in time contrived to grow from the smallest of nations into the greatest, and from the most obscure into the most renowned—through their humane reception of those in need of a dwelling among them, through their grant of citizenship to such as they nobly overcame in war, through their allowance that any slaves freed among them might be citizens, and through their disdain of no man's fortune, if only it might benefit the commonwealth; and, above all these things, through the good order of their government, which they established out of many sufferings, drawing some profit from every occasion. 10.1. As for the Aborigines, from whom the Roman race derives its origin, some declare them to be aboriginal inhabitants of Italy, a people sprung from the soil itself. (By Italy I mean the whole coastal land enclosed by the Ionian Gulf, the Tyrrhenian Sea, and, on the third side, by the Alps from the landward direction.) And they say that this first name was given them because they were the originators of birth to those who came after—as we might say "founders of a race" or "first-born." 10.2. Others say that certain homeless wanderers, gathering together from many places, met one another there by some divine guidance and established their dwellings upon the heights, living by brigandage and by pasturing flocks. And these alter the name as well, to one more suited to their fortunes, calling them Aberrigines, so that they are shown to be wanderers. By this account the tribe of the Aborigines comes near to differing in nothing from those whom the ancients called Leleges; for it was upon homeless and mingled peoples, who dwelt in no land firmly held as a fatherland, that this name was for the most part bestowed. 10.3. Others tell in legend that they were colonists of the Ligurians who border on the Umbrians; for the Ligurians inhabit many parts of Italy, and occupy some part of Celtica as well. Which of the two is their native land is uncertain; for nothing further is said about them with any clarity. 11.1. But the most learned of the Roman historians—among whom is Porcius Cato, who compiled with the greatest care the genealogies of the cities in Italy, and Gaius Sempronius, and many others—say that they were Greeks, of those who once dwelt in Achaea, having migrated many generations before the Trojan War. They do not, however, further define either the Greek tribe to which they belonged, or the city from which they removed, or the time, or the leader of the colony, or the fortunes by which they left their mother-city; and although they have employed a Greek tradition, they have produced none of the writers of Greek history to confirm it. What the truth may be is therefore uncertain; but if their account is sound, the Aborigines could be colonists of no other race than that now called the Arcadian. 11.2. For these were the first of the Greeks to cross the Ionian Gulf and settle in Italy, led by Oenotrus, the son of Lycaon; and he was the fifth in descent from Aezeius and Phoroneus, the first to hold sway in the Peloponnese. For of Phoroneus was born Niobe; and her son by Zeus, as is told, was Pelasgus; and the son of Aezeius was Lycaon; and his daughter was Deianeira; and from Deianeira and Pelasgus sprang a second Lycaon; and his son was Oenotrus, seventeen generations before those who marched against Troy. Such, then, was the time at which the Greeks sent out their colony to Italy. 11.3. Oenotrus removed from Greece because he was not content with his portion; for Lycaon having had two-and-twenty sons, the land of the Arcadians had to be divided into as many shares. For this reason, then, Oenotrus left the Peloponnese, equipped a fleet, and crossed the Ionian Sea, and with him Peucetius, one of his brothers. Many of their own people followed them—for this nation is said to have been numerous in its beginnings—and so did such other Greeks as had less land than sufficed them. 11.4. Peucetius, then, where they first put in along the coast of Italy, above the Iapygian promontory, disembarked his people and settled there; and from him those who dwell about that region were called Peucetians. But Oenotrus, leading the greater part of the host, came to the other gulf that washes the western side of Italy—which was then called Ausonian, from the Ausonians who dwelt beside it, but afterwards, when the Tyrrhenians became masters of the sea, took the name it now bears. 12.1. Finding a land much of it well suited to pasturage and much to tillage, but for the most part desolate, and even the inhabited part not populous, he cleared away the barbarian element from a portion of it and founded small cities, close together, upon the heights, this being the manner of habitation customary among the ancients. And the whole land, vast as it was, that he held came to be called Oenotria, and all the men over whom he ruled were called Oenotrians—this being the third name they had taken. For under the reign of Aezeius they were called Aezeians; when Lycaon succeeded to the rule, they were named Lycaonians after him; and when Oenotrus brought them into Italy, they were for a time called Oenotrians. 12.2. Sophocles the tragic poet bears witness to my account in his play Triptolemus; for Demeter is there represented as instructing Triptolemus how great a land he will be compelled to traverse, sowing it with the fruits she has given him. Mentioning first the eastern part of Italy—which runs from the Iapygian promontory to the Sicilian strait—and then touching upon Sicily over against it, she turns back again to the western part of Italy and goes through the greatest of the nations inhabiting that coast, making her beginning from the dwelling-place of the Oenotrians. It will suffice to cite these iambic lines alone, in which she says: "And what lies behind, on the right hand, all Oenotria and the Tyrrhenian Gulf, and the land of Liguria, shall receive you." 12.3. And Antiochus of Syracuse, a very ancient historian, in his work On the Settlement of Italy, recounting the most ancient inhabitants and what part of it each held, says that the Oenotrians were the first of those recorded to dwell in it, speaking thus: "Antiochus son of Xenophanes wrote this concerning Italy, the most trustworthy and clearest things out of the ancient accounts: this land, which is now called Italy, the Oenotrians held of old." Then, having gone through the manner in which they were governed, and how in time a king named Italus arose among them, from whom they were renamed Italians, and how Morges succeeded to his rule, from whom they were called Morgetes, and how Sicelus, being received as a guest by Morges and exercising a rule of his own, divided the nation, he adds these words: "Thus the Sicels and the Morgetes and the Italietes came to be, being Oenotrians." 13.1. Come now, let me show the stock from which the Oenotrians sprang, producing as witness another of the ancient historians, Pherecydes of Athens, second to none of the genealogists. For there is given by him this account concerning those who reigned in Arcadia: "Of Pelasgus and Deianeira is born Lycaon; this man marries Cyllene, a Naiad nymph, from whom the mountain Cyllene takes its name." Then, going through those born of these and the regions each settled, he makes mention of Oenotrus and Peucetius, saying thus: "And Oenotrus, from whom are called Oenotrians those who dwell in Italy, and Peucetius, from whom are called Peucetians those on the Ionian Gulf." 13.2. Such, then, is what has been said by the ancient poets and writers of legend concerning the dwelling-place and origin of the Oenotrians. Trusting in them, if indeed the Aborigines were a Greek tribe, as Cato and Sempronius and many others have stated, I suppose them to be descendants of these very Oenotrians. For the Pelasgian and the Cretan stocks, and whatever others settled in Italy, I find to have come in later times; and an expedition earlier than this, removing from Greece into the western parts of Europe, I am unable to discover. 13.3. The Oenotrians, I believe, occupied many regions of the rest of Italy, seizing some that were desolate and others that were poorly inhabited; and they also cut off a portion of the land of the Umbrians, and were called Aborigines from their dwelling in the mountains (for it is an Arcadian trait to delight in mountains), just as at Athens men are called highlanders and coast-dwellers. 13.4. But if any are by nature not too quick to accept without examination what is said about ancient matters, let them be in no haste, either, to suppose these men Ligurians or Umbrians or some other barbarians; rather let them wait to learn the rest as well, and then judge from the whole what is most probable. 14.1. Of the cities in which the Aborigines first dwelt, few survived in my day; the greater part, ruined by wars and other calamities, have been abandoned and left desolate. They lay in the territory of Reate, not far from the Apennine mountains, as Terentius Varro writes in his Antiquities, the nearest being a day's journey distant from the city of Rome at the shortest. The most notable of them I shall describe, as he records them. 14.2. Palatium, distant five-and-twenty stades from Reate (a city still inhabited by Romans even in my time), near the Quintian Way. Tribola, distant about sixty stades from the same city, set upon a moderate hill. Suesbola, the same distance from Tribola, near the Ceraunian mountains. Forty stades from this is the notable city of Suna, where there is a very ancient temple of Ares. 14.3. Mephyla, about thirty stades away from Suna; its ruins and the traces of its wall are shown. Forty stades distant from Mephyla is Orvinium, as notable and great as any other of the cities of that region; for there are visible the foundations of its walls, certain tombs of an ancient fashion, and the circuits of common burial-places stretching along upon lofty mounds. There too is an ancient temple of Athena, set upon the height. 14.4. Eighty stades from Reate, for those who go by the Curian Way past Mount Coretus, is Corsula, lately destroyed. And there is shown an island, named Issa, surrounded by a lake, which men are said to have inhabited without any artificial defence, using the marshes of the lake in place of walls. Near Issa is Maruvium, lying at the inmost recess of the same lake, distant forty stades from the place called the Seven Waters. 14.5. Going again from Reate along the Latin road, one comes to Batia at thirty stades, and at three hundred to Tiora, called Matiene. In this city there is said to have been a very ancient oracle of Ares. Its manner, they say, was much like that which legend tells once existed among the Dodonaeans; save that there, upon a sacred oak, a dove was said to sit and utter prophecies, while among the Aborigines a heaven-sent bird, which they call picus and the Greeks woodpecker, appearing upon a wooden pillar, did the same. 14.6. Four-and-twenty stades from the aforesaid city is Lista, the mother-city of the Aborigines, which the Sabines, marching against it by night from the city of Amiternum, took unguarded in still earlier times. Those who survived the capture, being received by the people of Reate, when after many attempts they were unable to recover it, dedicated the land as still their own, consecrating it to the gods and laying curses upon any who should thereafter reap its fruits. 15.1. Seventy stades from Reate is the notable city of Cotylia, lying upon a mountain; not far from it is a lake four plethra in extent, full of a natural spring that flows perpetually, and of a depth said to be unfathomable. The inhabitants, holding it sacred to Victory and having something of the divine about it, fence it about with garlands so that no man may approach the water, and keep it inviolable, save at certain yearly seasons when those to whom it is lawful, stepping upon the little island within it, perform the customary sacrifices. 15.2. The island is about fifty feet in diameter, and rises above the water no more than a foot in height; it is not fixed, but floats about, drifting now to one place and now to another as the breeze gently turns it. A herbage like sedge grows upon it, with certain small shrubs—a thing beyond the telling for those who have not beheld what Nature does, and second to no marvel. 16.1. In these regions, then, the Aborigines are said to have made their first settlement, having driven out the Umbrians from them. Setting out from here, they made war over the land upon the other barbarians and most of all upon the Sicels, who were their neighbours. First a band of sacred youth went forth—a few men sent out by their parents in search of a livelihood, fulfilling an ancient custom which I know many barbarians and Greeks to have observed. 16.2. For whenever the cities of some peoples increased to such a multitude that their native produce no longer sufficed for all, or when the land, afflicted by changes of the heavens, brought forth its accustomed fruits but scantily, or when some other such circumstance, whether for better or for worse, imposed upon the cities the necessity of reducing their numbers, they would dedicate to some one of the gods the men born in a given year, and send them forth, equipped with arms, out of their own land. If they were rendering thank-offerings to the gods for an increase of population or for victory in war, they would first offer the customary sacrifices and send the colonies forth with auspicious omens; but if they were seeking, on account of divine wrath, deliverance from the evils that beset them, they would do the like, themselves grieving and asking pardon of those whom they drove away. 16.3. And these emigrants, knowing that they would no longer share in their fathers' land unless they should win another, made the land that received them—whether in friendship or conquered in war—their fatherland. And the god to whom they had been dedicated at their departure was generally thought to lend them aid, and, beyond human expectation, to bring their colonies to a prosperous issue. 16.4. Following this custom, then, certain of the Aborigines also at that time, their territories being full of men (for they thought it right to slay none of their offspring, holding this no less than a pollution), dedicated to some god the men born in a given year, and, when these had come to manhood, sent them forth as colonists out of their own land; and these, after they had left their own country, continued to harry and plunder the Sicels. 16.5. And once these had gained possession of certain places in the enemy's land, the rest of the Aborigines too, those who needed land, now from a more secure footing each on their own account attacked their neighbours and founded other cities, including those inhabited to this day—the Antemnates, the Tellenes, the Ficolneans near the mountains called Cornicula, and the Tiburtines, among whom even down to the present time a part of the city is named Sicelian. And of all the neighbouring peoples they were the most troublesome to the Sicels. From these quarrels there arose a war between whole nations, greater than any that had before occurred in Italy, and it advanced, dragging on through a long time. 17.1. Thereafter certain of the Pelasgians, who dwelt in what is now called Thessaly, being compelled to leave their own land, became fellow-settlers with the Aborigines and made war in common with them against the Sicels. The Aborigines received them, perhaps in the hope of profit, but, as I am persuaded, 17.2. most of all on account of their kinship. For the race of the Pelasgians too was Greek, of old from the Peloponnese; and it met with ill-starred fortunes in many things, but above all in its much-wandering habitation, fixed in no place. For first they dwelt about what is now called Achaean Argos, being natives of the soil, as the many say of them. And they took this name at the outset from 17.3. King Pelasgus. Now Pelasgus was the son of Zeus, as is told, and of Niobe daughter of Phoroneus, with whom, as the legend has it, Zeus first lay among mortal women. In the sixth generation thereafter, leaving the Peloponnese, they removed to the land then called Haemonia and now Thessaly; and the leaders of the colony were Achaeus and Phthius and Pelasgus, the sons of Larisa and Poseidon. Coming to Haemonia, they drove out the barbarians dwelling in it and divided the land into three parts, naming the portions after the leaders—Phthiotis, Achaia, and Pelasgiotis. And after remaining there five generations, in which they advanced to the height of prosperity, reaping the finest of the plains in Thessaly, about the sixth generation they were driven out of Thessaly by the Curetes and Leleges, who are now called Aetolians and Locrians, and by many others dwelling about Parnassus, the leader of their enemies being Deucalion the son of Prometheus, his mother being Clymene the daughter of Ocean. 18.1. Scattered in their flight, some departed to Crete, some seized certain of the Cyclades islands, some settled the region about Olympus and Ossa, called Hestiaeotis, others were carried over into Boeotia and Phocis and Euboea; while those who crossed into Asia seized many places along the coast about the Hellespont and many of the islands lying near it, among them the one now called Lesbos, mingling with those who sent the first colony into it under the leadership of Macar the son of Crinacus. 18.2. But the greater part of them, turning through the interior toward their kinsmen dwelling in Dodona—on whom no one thought it right to make war, as they were sacred—remained there for a fitting time. But when they perceived that they were a burden, since the land was not sufficient to nourish all, they left the country in obedience to an oracle that bade them sail to Italy, which was then called Saturnia. 18.3. Having built many ships, they crossed the Ionian Sea, eager to reach the parts of Italy nearest to them; but borne too far out by a south wind and by ignorance of the regions, and putting in at one of the mouths of the Po, called the Spinetic, they there left their ships and the portion of the multitude least able to endure hardship, setting a guard over them, so that they might have a refuge if 18.4. matters should not go forward for them. And those who stayed behind in this place, having thrown a wall about the camp and brought in from the ships the provisions for their livelihood, when their affairs seemed to be going according to their wishes, founded a city of the same name as the mouth of the river; and they prospered, beyond any of those dwelling about the Ionian Sea, holding the mastery of the sea for a long time, and they sent up to Delphi, to the god, tithes of their gains from the sea, 18.5. as brilliant as any men ever sent. Later, however, when the neighbouring barbarians marched against them with a great force, they abandoned the city; and the barbarians in turn were in time driven out by the Romans. Thus the branch of the Pelasgians left behind at Spina perished. 19.1. But those who had turned through the interior, crossing the mountainous part of Italy, came to the land of the Umbrians, who bordered upon the Aborigines. The Umbrians inhabited many other regions of Italy as well, and this nation was among the very great and ancient. At first the Pelasgians held the places where they first established themselves, and seized some of the small towns of the Umbrians; but when a great army gathered against them, fearing the multitude of their enemies, they turned and withdrew into the land of the Aborigines. 19.2. And the Aborigines thought it right to treat them as enemies, and gathered in haste from the nearest places to drive them out. But the Pelasgians—who chanced at this time, by some divine guidance, to be encamped near the city of Cotylia of the Aborigines, beside the sacred lake—when they observed the little island whirling about within it, and heard from the captives whom they had taken from the fields the name of the inhabitants, supposed that the oracle had found its fulfilment for them. 19.3. For the oracle that had been given them at Dodona—which Lucius Mallius, a man of no obscure note, says he himself saw engraved in ancient letters upon one of the tripods set within the precinct of Zeus—ran thus: "Go, seeking the Saturnian land of the Sicels and the Cotyle of the Aborigines, where an island floats; mingling with these, send forth a tithe to Phoebus, and heads to the son of Cronus, and to the father send a man." 20.1. When, then, the Aborigines had come with a great army, the Pelasgians, holding out suppliant boughs, advanced to meet them unarmed, telling of their own fortunes and entreating them to receive them in friendship as fellow-settlers who would not be a burden, since the divine power was leading them to this land alone—expounding to them the oracle. 20.2. And the Aborigines, when they heard these things, resolved to obey the oracle and to gain a Greek alliance against the barbarians at variance with them, being hard pressed in their war against the Sicels. So they made a treaty with the Pelasgians and gave them lands cut off from their own, about the sacred lake, where most of the ground was marshy—lands now called, after the ancient manner of speech, Velia. 20.3. For it was customary with the ancient Greeks for the most part to set before names whose beginnings were from vowels the syllable "ou," written with a single letter. This was like a gamma, with two oblique strokes joined upon one upright, as in wHelen and 20.4. wAnax and wOikos and wAer and many such. Then a portion of them, and that no small one, since the land did not suffice for all, having persuaded the Aborigines to assist them in the expedition, marched against the Umbrians and, falling suddenly upon a prosperous and great city of theirs, took Croton. Using this as a fortress and stronghold against the Umbrians—it being equipped sufficiently to serve as a bulwark in war and having the surrounding country good for grazing—they gained possession of many other places besides, and continued with great zeal to help the Aborigines carry on the war against the Sicels, which was still in progress, until they drove them out of their land. 20.5. And the Pelasgians, in common with the Aborigines, inhabited many cities, some previously dwelt in by the Sicels, others built by themselves; among them is the city of the Caeretans, then called Agylla, and Pisa and Saturnia and Alsium and certain others, which in time were taken from them by the Tyrrhenians. 21.1. Falerium and Fescennium were still inhabited by Romans down to my own day, preserving some small embers of the Pelasgian race, having formerly belonged to the Sicels. In these cities many of the ancient usages once practised by the Greeks survived for a very long time: such as the fashion of their warlike arms—Argolic shields and spears; and that, whenever they began a war or repelled invaders by sending an army beyond their borders, certain sacred men went unarmed before the rest as bearers of truces; and the construction of their temples and the images of the gods, their rites of consecration and sacrifices, and many other such things. 21.2. But the most conspicuous monument of the former dwelling at Argos of those men who drove out the Sicels is the temple of Hera at Falerium, built as it was at Argos; where the manner of the sacrifices too was the same, and there were sacred women tending the precinct, and the so-called basket-bearer, a maiden pure of marriage, beginning the rites of sacrifice, and choirs of maidens hymning the goddess in ancestral songs. 21.3. These also obtained no small portion of the plains called Campanian, very good for pasturage and most pleasant to behold, having in part driven out a barbarian people, the Auronissi; and they built cities there, including Larisa, to which they gave the name of their mother-city in the Peloponnese. 21.4. Now of the other small towns some were still standing down to my time, though they had often changed their inhabitants; but Larisa, desolate from very ancient times, has no clear sign to those now living that it was ever inhabited at all, save its name—and not even that do many know. It was not far from what is called the Popilian market. They also held many other places, both along the coast and in the interior, having taken them from the Sicels. 22.1. The Sicels—for they were no longer able to hold out, being warred upon by the Pelasgians and the Aborigines—gathered up their children and wives and such of their goods as were gold or silver, and gave up the whole land to them. Turning through the mountainous country toward the south and passing through all the lower part of Italy, since they were everywhere driven on, in time they constructed rafts at the strait and, watching for the current to run down from Italy, crossed over to the nearest 22.2. island. It was held by the Sicani, an Iberian people, who had not long before settled in it, fleeing from the Ligurians, and who caused the island, formerly called Trinacria from its triangular shape, to be named Sicania after themselves. There were not many inhabitants in it, great as it was, but the greater part of the land was still desolate. The Sicels, then, brought down into it, dwelt first in the western parts, and afterwards in many other regions as well; and from them the island began at 22.3. that time to be called Sicilia. Thus the Sicel race left Italy—as Hellanicus of Lesbos says, in the third generation before the Trojan War, in the twenty-sixth year of the priesthood of Alcyone at Argos. He makes two Italic expeditions cross into Sicily: the earlier of the Elymians, whom he says were driven out by the Oenotrians; and the second, occurring five years afterward, of the Ausonians fleeing the Iapygians. He declares their king to have been Sicelus, from whom the name was given both to the people and to the island. 22.4. But as Philistus of Syracuse wrote, the time of the crossing was the eightieth year before the Trojan War, and the people brought over from Italy was neither that of the Sicels nor of the Ausonians nor of the Elymians, but of the Ligurians, led by Sicelus; and this man, he says, was the son of Italus, and the people were named Sicels in his reign. 22.5. And the Ligurians, he says, were driven from their own land by the Umbrians and the Pelasgians. Antiochus of Syracuse does not make clear the time of the crossing, but declares those who migrated to be Sicels, forced out by the Oenotrians and Opicans, having made Straton the leader of their colony. Thucydides writes that those who migrated were Sicels, that those who expelled them were Opicans, and that the time was many years after the Trojan War. Such, then, are the accounts given by writers of note concerning the Sicels who transferred their habitation from Italy to Sicily. 23.1. The Pelasgians, having gained possession of much good land, taking over many cities and building others themselves, made a great and rapid advance in population, wealth, and other prosperity—of which, however, they enjoyed no long benefit. For at the very time when they seemed in all things to flourish, driven on by certain divine wraths, some perished by visitations of heaven, others by the neighbouring barbarians; and the greater part of them were again scattered into Greece and into barbarian lands (of whom there would be much to say, if I wished to write the matter exactly), while a small remnant stayed in Italy through the providence of the Aborigines. 23.2. First, then, the ruin of the cities seemed to begin with the land's being afflicted by drought, when no fruit ripened upon the trees and remained, but they fell down unripe; nor did such seeds as sent up shoots and came to flower fulfil their due time until the ripening of the ear; nor did grass grow sufficient for the cattle; and of the streams, some were no longer wholesome to drink, others failed in summer, 23.3. and others were wholly dried up. Things akin to these befell the breeding of flocks and of women; for either the embryos were miscarried, or they perished in the very birth, in some cases destroying together with them the mothers that bore them. And if any escaped the danger of the pangs, it was maimed, or imperfect, or harmed by some other mischance, and was not fit to be reared. Then the rest of the people too, especially those in their prime, were afflicted by diseases and by deaths beyond the natural number. 23.4. When they inquired of the oracle which of the gods or divine powers they had transgressed against, that they suffered these things, and what they might do for the terrors to abate, the god replied that, having obtained what they wished, they had not rendered what they had vowed, but still owed the things of greatest worth. 23.5. For the Pelasgians, when there had come upon them a barrenness of their land in all produce, had vowed to Zeus and Apollo and the Cabeiri to sacrifice tithes of all that should thereafter be born to them; but when the vow was fulfilled, they set apart and offered to the gods the portion of fruits and of cattle alone, as though they had vowed concerning these only. This Myrsilus of Lesbos has recorded, writing in almost the same words as I do now, save that he does not call the men Pelasgians but Tyrrhenians; the reason for which I shall give a little later. 24.1. When they learned the oracle that had been brought back, they could not interpret what was said. While they were at a loss, one of the elders, interpreting the response, said that they had wholly erred if they thought the gods were accusing them unjustly; for of their goods all the first-fruits had been rendered rightly and with justice, but the portion of human offspring—a thing most precious of all to the gods—was still owed; and if they should receive this just share too, the response would find fulfilment for them. 24.2. To some this seemed rightly said, but to others the argument seemed framed from a plot; and when someone proposed the suggestion that they ask the god whether it was pleasing to him to receive tithes of men, they sent envoys a second time, and the god replied that they should so do. Thereupon dissension fell upon them concerning the manner of the tithing. And first those who presided over the cities were thrown into confusion among themselves; 24.3. then the rest of the people too took the magistrates in suspicion. And the departures took place in no order, but, as was natural, as men driven on by frenzy and divine affliction; and many whole households were blotted out when a part of their members removed, since their kinsmen did not think it right to be left bereft of their dearest and to remain among their bitterest enemies. 24.4. These, then, were the first to migrate from Italy and to wander into Greece and over much of the barbarian world. And after the first, others suffered the same, and this continued to happen every year; for those in power in the cities did not cease to set apart the first-fruits of the youth that was ever coming to manhood, both thinking it right to render the gods their due and fearing dissensions on the part of those who had escaped notice. There was also much that was driven out, under a specious pretext, through enmity on the part of those at variance with one another; so that the departures were many, and the Pelasgian race was scattered over the greatest extent of the earth. 25.1. In matters of war they were better than many, since they had made their training amid dangers, living among warlike nations; and in nautical skill they had advanced very far through their dwelling with the Tyrrhenians; and necessity, which is sufficient to furnish daring to men destitute of a livelihood, became their leader and teacher in every venture, 25.2. so that they prevailed without difficulty wherever they went. And they were called by other men, by the appellation of the country from which they had set out and by the memory of their ancient stock, the same men both Tyrrhenians and Pelasgians. Of which I have made mention, that no one may marvel, whenever he hears poets or historians naming the Pelasgians and the Tyrrhenians, how the same men came to bear both names. 25.3. For concerning them Thucydides has a clear mention of the Thracian promontory and the cities lying upon it, which men of two tongues inhabit. And concerning the Pelasgian nation his words are these: "There is in it also something Chalcidic, but the greatest part is Pelasgic, of the Tyrrhenians who once inhabited Lemnos and Athens." 25.4. And in Sophocles, in the play Inachus, an anapaestic verse spoken by the chorus is composed thus: "Inachus the giver, child of the father of springs, Ocean, holding great precedence over the plains of Argos and the hills of Hera, and over the Tyrsenian Pelasgians." 25.5. For the name of Tyrrhenia was at that time spread through Greece, and all of western Italy, stripped of the appellations of its several peoples, took on that designation—just as happened in many other parts of Greece, and about what is now called the Peloponnese. For from one of the peoples dwelling in it, the Achaean, the whole peninsula—in which are the Arcadian and the Ionian and many other peoples—was named Achaia. 26.1. The time at which the Pelasgian race began to suffer was about the second generation before the Trojan War; and it extended even after the Trojan War, until the people was reduced to the smallest number. For except Croton, a city of note among the Umbrians, and whatever else happened to have been settled in the land of the Aborigines, the rest of the Pelasgian towns were destroyed. Croton long preserved its ancient form; but it is not long since it changed both its name and its inhabitants, and now it is a Roman colony, and is called 26.2. Corthonia. Those who took over the cities of the Pelasgians who had left the country were many others, as each happened to have their dwellings bordering on certain places, but most of all, the most numerous and the best, the Tyrrhenians. Some declare the Tyrrhenians to be natives of Italy, others newcomers. And this appellation those who make the people indigenous say was given them from the strongholds which they, first of those dwelling there, constructed; for among the Tyrrhenians too, walled and roofed dwellings are called towers (tyrseis), as among the Greeks. From what befell them, then, they hold the name to have been given, just as to the Mosynoeci in Asia; for those too dwell upon high palisades like wooden towers, calling them mosynes. 27.1. But those who tell in legend that they were immigrants declare that Tyrrhenus, having become the leader of the colony, gave the people their name from himself; and that he was a Lydian by race, from the country formerly called Maeonia, being some ancient immigrant. And he was fifth in descent from Zeus, they say, holding that from Zeus and Earth was born Manes, the first king in this land; and of him and Callirrhoe daughter of Ocean was begotten Cotys; and to Cotys, who married Halie the daughter of Tyllus the earth-born, were born two sons, Asies and Atys; 27.2. and of Atys and Callithea daughter of Choraeus sprang Lydus and Tyrrhenus; and Lydus, remaining there, took over his father's rule, and from him the land was named Lydia; while Tyrrhenus, having led the colony, gained much of Italy and gave this appellation to those who shared in his expedition. 27.3. By Herodotus the family of Tyrrhenus are called sons of Atys the son of Manes, and the migration of the Maeonians into Italy was not voluntary. For he says that in the reign of Atys there came a barrenness of produce upon the land of the Maeonians, and that the people, while at first held back by their love of country, devised many remedies against the calamity—on one day taking moderate food, on the next enduring without; but when the distress dragged on, they divided the whole people in two and cast lots upon the portions, one for departure from the country, the other for remaining, and of the sons of Atys assigned one to the one part and the other to the other. 27.4. And when the portion that was with Lydus drew the lot of remaining, the other, having received its share of the goods, withdrew; and putting in at the western parts of Italy, where the Umbrians had their dwelling, it remained there and founded the cities still existing in his very day. 28.1. I know that many other historians too have made use of this account concerning the race of the Tyrrhenians—some in the same terms, others altering the settlement and the time. For some said that Tyrrhenus was the son of Heracles by Omphale the Lydian, and that he, coming to Italy, drove the Pelasgians out of the cities—not all of them, but those that were beyond the Tiber in the northern part. Others declare Tyrrhenus to be the son of Telephus, and that he came to Italy after the capture of Troy. 28.2. But Xanthus the Lydian, a man as well versed in ancient history as any other, and one who would be reckoned no less a confirmer of his country's traditions than any, has nowhere in his writing named Tyrrhenus as a ruler of the Lydians, nor does he know of a colony of the Maeonians taking possession of Italy, nor has he made any mention of Tyrrhenia, though he mentions other less notable foundations of the Lydians. He says that the sons of Atys were Lydus and Torebus, and that these, having divided their father's rule, both remained in Asia; and that the peoples over whom they ruled received their names from them, speaking thus: "From Lydus come the Lydians, from Torebus the Torebians. Their speech differs a little, and even now they mock one another with no few words, as do the Ionians and 28.3. the Dorians." But Hellanicus of Lesbos says that the Tyrrhenians, formerly called Pelasgians, took the appellation they now have when they settled in Italy. And his account in the Phoronis runs thus: "Of Pelasgus their king and of Menippe daughter of Peneus was born Phrastor, and of him Amyntor, and of him Teutamides, and of him Nanas. In his reign the Pelasgians were driven out by the Greeks, and leaving their ships at the river Spinetus in the Ionian Gulf, they took Croton, a city in the interior, and setting out from there they founded what is now called Tyrsenia." 28.4. But Myrsilus, declaring the contrary to Hellanicus, says that the Tyrrhenians, when they had left their own land, were in their wandering renamed Pelargi (storks), being likened to the birds called storks, since they roved in flocks both into Greece and into barbarian lands; and that these built for the Athenians the wall about the Acropolis, called the Pelargic. 29.1. To me, however, all those seem to err who have been persuaded that the Tyrrhenian and the Pelasgian are one and the same people. That they should once have shared in each other's name was nothing to marvel at, since certain other peoples too, some Greek, some barbarian, have suffered the same—as the Trojan and the Phrygian, dwelling near one another (indeed by many both these were thought one race, differing in name and not in nature); and not least among those elsewhere blended together by likeness of names are the peoples in Italy. 29.2. For there was a time when the Latins and the Umbrians and the Ausonians and many others too were called Tyrrhenians by the Greeks, the distance of the peoples' habitation making the exact truth obscure to those far off; and many of the historians supposed Rome itself to be a Tyrrhenian city. The interchange of names, then, since also of ways of life, I am persuaded befell these peoples; but that both partook of a common race I am not persuaded, judging from many other things, and most of all from their tongues, which are different and preserve no likeness whatever. 29.3. "For neither," as Herodotus says, "are the Crotoniates of like speech with any of those who now dwell about them, nor the Placiani; but they are of like speech with one another. And they make it plain that the character of speech they brought with them when they removed into these regions they keep under guard." And yet one might marvel that the Crotoniates had a dialect like that of the Placiani dwelling about the Hellespont, since both were Pelasgians from the first, but none at all like that of the Tyrrhenians who dwell nearest them. For if kinship is to be supposed the cause of likeness of speech, surely the other—diversity of speech—is the mark of the absence of kinship; 29.4. for it is not possible to hold both on the same principle. And indeed the one would even have had some reason for occurring—namely that men of the same race, having made their habitations far from one another, no longer preserved the same character of dialect, on account of their intercourse with their neighbours; but that men dwelling in the same regions should agree in nothing whatever in speech, if sprung from the same race, has no reason at all. 30.1. Using this proof, then, I am persuaded that the Pelasgians are a people distinct from the Tyrrhenians. Nor indeed do I think that the Tyrrhenians were colonists of the Lydians; for neither are they of like speech with them, nor can it be said that, though they no longer use a similar tongue, they yet preserve certain other tokens of their mother-city. For they neither hold the same gods as the Lydians, nor do they use similar laws or pursuits; rather, in these very things they differ more from the Lydians than from the Pelasgians. 30.2. For they come nearer to speaking what resembles the truth who declare the people to have come from nowhere, but to be native, since it is found to be very ancient and of like tongue and like manner of life with no other race. Nothing, however, prevents its having been named by the Greeks with this appellation, both on account of its dwellings in towers and 30.3. from a man who was its ruler. The Romans, however, call it by other names; for from the country in which it once dwelt, called Etruria, they call the men Etruscans; and from their experience in the ministrations concerning divine worship, in which they surpass others, they now call them, less precisely, Tusci, but formerly, getting the name exactly, they called them, as the Greeks do, Thyoscoi (sacrificers). They themselves, however, call themselves, after one of their leaders, Rasenna, in the same manner as that man. 30.4. What cities the Tyrrhenians founded, what orders of government they established, how great a power they all had, what deeds worthy of record they accomplished, and what fortunes befell them, shall be set forth in another work. 30.5. The Pelasgian tribe, then—so much of it as was not destroyed and scattered among the colonies, but remained, a small remnant of a great host, sharing in government with the Aborigines—was left behind in these regions, where in time their descendants, together with the others, built Rome. Such, then, are the legends told concerning the Pelasgian race. 31.1. Not long afterward another Greek expedition came down into these regions of Italy, about sixty years before the Trojan War, as the Romans themselves say, having set out from the Arcadian city of Pallantium. The leader of the colony was Evander, said to be the son of Hermes and of a certain nymph native to the Arcadians, whom the Greeks say was Themis and declare to have been inspired, but those who have written the Roman antiquities name in the native tongue Carmenta. The name of the nymph would be, in the Greek tongue, Thespiodos (singer of prophecies); for the Romans call songs carmina, and they agree that this woman, being possessed by a divine spirit, foretold to the people through song the things that were to come to pass. 31.2. This expedition was not sent forth by common consent, but, the people having fallen into discord, the defeated party withdrew willingly. It chanced that at that time Faunus had received the kingdom of the Aborigines, a descendant, they say, of Ares, a man both active and prudent, whom the Romans honour with sacrifices and songs as one of the native divinities. This man, receiving the Arcadians, who were few, with much friendship, gave them as much of his own land as they wished. 31.3. And the Arcadians, as Themis, prophesying to them, directed, chose a hill a little distance from the Tiber, which is now about the middle of the city of Rome, and built near it a small village, sufficient for the two ships' companies with which they had come from Greece—a village which fate was in time to make so great that no Greek or barbarian city should surpass it in size of habitation, in dignity of dominion, and in all other prosperity, and that, for as long as mortal life endures, 31.4. it should be remembered above almost all cities. They gave this town the name Pallantium, after their mother-city in Arcadia; now, however, it is called by the Romans Palatium, time having confounded the exact form and furnishing many men occasions for absurd etymologies. 32.1. But as some relate, among whom is also Polybius of Megalopolis, it was named after a youth, Pallas, who died there; and this youth was the son of Heracles and of Launa, the daughter of Evander; and his grandfather, having heaped up a tomb for him upon the hill, named the place Pallantium after the youth. 32.2. I, however, have neither beheld any tomb of Pallas in Rome, nor learned of libations being performed, nor been able to see anything else of the sort, although this house is not left unremembered, nor without a share of the honours with which the divine race is honoured by men. For I have learned that sacrifices are performed by the Romans to Evander every year at public charge, and to Carmenta, just as to the other heroes and divinities, and I have beheld altars set up—to Carmenta beneath what is called the Capitol, beside the Carmental gates, and to Evander beside another of the hills, called the Aventine, not far from the Triple gate; but to Pallas 32.3. I know of none of these things being done. The Arcadians, then, settled together beneath the hill, ordered the foundation in other respects according to their native customs, and set up shrines—first to Lycaean Pan, at the direction of Themis (for among the Arcadians Pan is the oldest and most honoured of the gods)—having found a fitting place, which the Romans call the Lupercal, and we should call the Lycaeum. 32.4. Now indeed, since the surrounding places have been built up together with the precinct, the ancient nature of the spot has become hard to conjecture; but of old, as is told, there was a great cave beneath the hill, roofed over with thick wood, and springs deep beneath the rocks, and the glen adjoining the cliff was shaded with dense and great trees. 32.5. There, having set up an altar to the god, they performed the ancestral sacrifice, which down to our own time the Romans offer in the month of February after the winter solstice, changing nothing of what was then done; the manner of the sacrifice shall be told hereafter. And upon the summit of the hill, having set apart the precinct of Victory, they established yearly sacrifices to her as well, which even in my day the Romans offered. 33.1. This goddess the Arcadians tell in legend to be the daughter of Pallas the son of Lycaon; and the honours she now has from men she received, they say, by the will of Athena, having been the foster-companion of the goddess. For Athena was given immediately from her birth to Pallas by Zeus, and was reared with him until she came to maturity. They also set up a shrine of Demeter and offered sacrifices to her through women and without wine, as is the custom among the Greeks, 33.2. of which our time has changed nothing. They also assigned a precinct to Poseidon Hippios and established the festival called Hippocrateia by the Arcadians but Consualia by the Romans, in which it is the custom among the Romans for horses and mules to rest from labour and to be wreathed about the head with flowers. 33.3. Many other precincts too, and altars and images of the gods, they consecrated, and they established ancestral rites and sacrifices, which down to my own times were performed in the same manner. I should not marvel, however, if some have been omitted, having escaped the memory of later generations through their very great antiquity; yet those still performed now suffice to be proofs of the Arcadian customs of old; but more shall be said of them elsewhere. 33.4. The Arcadians are also said to have been the first to bring into Italy the use of Greek letters, lately come to light, and music through instruments—those called lyres and triangles and pipes—since the earlier inhabitants used no other device of music save shepherds' reed-pipes; to have laid down laws, and to have brought their way of life for the most part from a beast-like state to gentleness; to have introduced arts and pursuits and many other benefits to the common stock; and on this account to have met with much care from those who received them. 33.5. This was the second Greek people to come, after the Pelasgians, into Italy, and it had a dwelling in common with the Aborigines, established in the strongest part of Rome. 34.1. A few years after the Arcadians, another Greek expedition came into Italy, led by Heracles, who came after subduing Iberia and all the lands as far as the setting of the sun. Some of his followers, having begged Heracles to be released from the campaign, remained about these regions and built a town, having found a fitting hill, separated from the Pallantium by about three stades in length, which is now called the Capitoline, but was called by the men of that time Saturnius—as one might say in the Greek tongue Cronius. 34.2. Of those left behind, the greater part were Peloponnesians—Pheneatae and Epeans from Elis—who had no longer any longing for the way home, their country having been laid waste in the war against Heracles; and there was mingled with them some Trojan element as well, of those taken captive from Ilium in the reign of Laomedon, when Heracles took the city. And it seems to me that of the rest of the host too, whatever was wearied or oppressed by the wandering, having begged release from the campaign, remained in this 34.3. place. As for the name of the hill, some think, as I said, that it is ancient, and that for this reason the Epeans not least delighted in the hill, in memory of the Cronian hill in Elis, which is in the land of Pisa near the river Alpheus, and which the Eleans, holding it sacred to Cronus, honour with sacrifices and other honours, gathering at appointed times. 34.4. But Euxenus, an ancient poet, and certain others of the Italian writers of legend think that the name was given to the place by the Pisatans themselves, on account of its likeness to the Cronium among them, and that the Epeans set up the altar to Cronus together with Heracles—which even now remains at the foot of the hill on the ascent leading from the forum to the Capitol—and that they were the ones who established the sacrifice which even in my day the Romans offered, keeping the Greek custom. 34.5. But as I find by inference, even before Heracles came to Italy the place was sacred to Cronus, called by the inhabitants Saturnius, and the whole rest of the coast now called Italy was dedicated to this god, being named Saturnia by those dwelling in it—as may be found stated in certain Sibylline oracles and other responses given by the gods; and shrines have been set up to the god in many parts of the country, and certain cities are named thus, as the whole coast then was, and many places bear the divinity's name, especially the crags and the heights. 35.1. But in time it was named Italy, after a man who was its ruler, named Italus. This man, Antiochus of Syracuse says, having become good and wise, and persuading some of his neighbours by words and bringing others over by force, made all the land subject to himself that lay within the gulfs of Napetus and Scylletium; and this was the first to be called Italy, after Italus. And when he had become master of this and had many men subject to him, he straightway reached out for the lands adjoining and gathered together many cities; and he was an Oenotrian by race. 35.2. But Hellanicus of Lesbos says that Heracles, when he was driving the cattle of Geryon to Argos, since one of the calves leapt away from the herd while he was now in Italy and, fleeing, ran through the coast and, swimming across the strait of sea between, came to Sicily, Heracles, ever asking the inhabitants among whom he came in his pursuit of the calf whether anyone had seen it—the men of that land understanding little of the Greek tongue, and in their native speech, in pointing out the animal, calling the calf vitulus, as it is called even now—named the whole land through which the calf passed, after the animal, 35.3. Vitulia. And it is no marvel that the name was changed in time to its present form, since many Greek names too have suffered the like. But whether, as Antiochus says, it took this name from a man who was its leader—which is perhaps the more probable—or, as Hellanicus thinks, from the bull, this at least is plain from both: that it was so named in the age of Heracles, or a little before. Before this, the Greeks called it Hesperia and Ausonia, and the inhabitants Saturnia, as I have said before. 36.1. There is also another account told in legend by the inhabitants: that before the reign of Zeus, Cronus held sway in this land, and that the life said to have been in his time, abundant in all that the seasons produce, was nowhere more so than among them. 36.2. And if anyone, otherwise removing the legendary part of the account, should wish to examine the excellence of a land from which the human race reaped the most numerous delights, having come into being—whether straightway from the earth, as the ancient account has it, or in some other way—he would find none more fitting than this. For, as one land is to be judged against another of so great a size, Italy is, in my opinion, the best, not only of Europe but of all the rest of the world. 36.3. And yet it does not escape me that to many I shall seem to say what is not credible, when they call to mind Egypt and Libya and Babylon and any other prosperous lands. But I do not reckon the wealth that comes from the earth in a single kind of produce, nor does an eagerness come upon me for a habitation in which there are only rich fields, but nothing else, or but little, that is useful; rather, whatever land may be most self-sufficient and least in need, for the most part, of imported goods, this I reckon the best. And that Italy is, beyond any other land, all-bearing and of much benefit, I am persuaded. 37.1. For it is not that she has good and many fields but is treeless, as one fit for corn; nor again that she is sufficient to nourish all manner of plants but is poor in fruit when sown, as one fit for trees; nor that she furnishes both these things in abundance but is unsuited for the pasturing of flocks; nor could anyone say that she is rich in fruit and trees and pasture, but an unpleasant dwelling-place for men; rather, she is, one may say, full of every delight and 37.2. benefit. For what corn-bearing land does she fall short of, when the plains of Campania, watered not by rivers but by the waters of heaven, fall short of none—in which I have beheld fields bearing three crops, producing a summer sowing upon a winter one and an autumn upon a summer? What olive-bearing land, when she has the farms of the Messapians and Daunians and Sabines and many others? What vine-planted land, when Tyrrhenia and the Alban country and the lands of the Falernians are marvellously fond of the vine, and able with the least labour to bring forth at once the most numerous and the finest fruits? 37.3. And apart from the land under cultivation, one would find much of it given over to flocks, and much to the grazing of goats, and still more—and more marvellous—to the rearing of horses and cattle; for the marsh and meadow herbage, being abundant, and the dewy and well-watered pastures, boundless in extent, are grazed in summer and furnish flourishing herds throughout the year. 37.4. But most marvellous of all are the forests about the steep regions and the glens and the untilled hills, from which they are supplied with much fine timber fit for shipbuilding, and much suited for other works. And of these nothing is hard to procure or lying far from human use, but all are easy to work and ready at hand, on account of the multitude of the rivers which flow through the whole coast and make the conveyance and exchange of the things that grow from the earth profitable. 37.5. The land has also springs of hot waters found in many places, to furnish baths most pleasant and to heal chronic diseases best of all, and mines of every kind, and abundant takings of game, and a sea of teeming fertility, and countless other things, some useful, some marvellous; and, finest of all, an air tempered with the seasons in due measure, such as least harms, by excesses of cold or extraordinary heats, the bringing-forth of fruits and the nature of living things. 38.1. No marvel was it, then, that the ancients held this land sacred to Cronus, deeming this divinity to be the giver and fulfiller to men of all happiness—whether one ought to call him Cronus, as the Greeks think fit, or Saturn, as the Romans, but one who embraces the whole nature of the universe, by whichever name one names him—and seeing this land full of all that abundance and grace which the mortal race desires; thinking too that to the divine and the mortal race alike there is a fitting portion, and that of all places this was the most suitable: the mountains and glens to Pan, the meadows and verdant places to the nymphs, the shores and islands to the divinities of the deep, and the rest, as each was 38.2. proper to some god and divinity. They say also that the ancients performed human sacrifices to Cronus, as was done at Carthage so long as that city endured, and as is done among the Celts to this day, and among certain others of the western peoples; and that Heracles, wishing to put a stop to the law of that sacrifice, both set up the altar upon the Saturnian hill and made beginning of pure offerings consecrated upon a clean fire; and that, so men might have no scruple, as having neglected their ancestral sacrifices, he taught the inhabitants to appease the wrath of the god—in place of the men whom they used to bind, render helpless of hand, and cast into the stream of the Tiber—by making images in the likeness of men, adorned in the same manner as those, and casting them into the river, so that whatever of dread remained in the souls of all might be removed, the likenesses of the ancient practice being still preserved. 38.3. This the Romans continued to do down to my own day, a little after the spring equinox, in the month of May, on what are called the Ides, wishing this to be the day of the full moon; on which, after offering the sacrifices prescribed by the laws, those called Pontifices, the most distinguished of the priests, and with them the maidens who guard the immortal fire, and the praetors, and such others of the citizens as it is lawful to be present at the rites, cast images fashioned in the likeness of men, thirty in number, from the sacred bridge into the stream of the Tiber, calling them 38.4. Argives. But concerning the sacrifices and the other rites which the city of Rome performs both after the Greek and after the native manner, we shall speak in another work; the present occasion seems rather to require that we go through the coming of Heracles to Italy with greater care, and not pass over anything worth recording that he did there. 39.1. Of the things told concerning this divinity, some are more legendary, others nearer the truth. The legendary account of his coming runs thus: that Heracles, commanded by Eurystheus, among his other labours, to drive the cattle of Geryon from Erytheia to Argos, having accomplished the labour and making his way homeward, came to many other parts of Italy and also to that region of the land of the Aborigines adjoining the Pallantium. 39.2. And finding there much fine pasture for cattle, he turned the cattle out to graze, and himself, weighed down with weariness, lay down and gave himself to sleep. Meanwhile a native robber, by name Cacus, came upon the cattle grazing unguarded and conceived a desire for them. And when he perceived Heracles sleeping there, thinking he could not drive off all of them undetected, and seeing too that the thing was not easy, he hid away a few of them in the cave in which he chanced to dwell near by, dragging each by the tail in the direction contrary to the natural course of the animals' walk; which could provide him concealment of the proofs, the track being made to appear opposite to the footprints. 39.3.
