Heracles, rising after a little and counting the number of the cattle, when he found some missing, was for a time at a loss whither they had gone, and, thinking them strayed from the pasture, sought them throughout the place; but when he could not find them, he came to the cave, baffled by the tracks, yet thinking he must none the less search the place. Cacus stood before the door, denying that he had seen the cattle when questioned, not allowing a search when asked, and crying out to his neighbours that he was being grievously treated by the stranger; whereupon Heracles, at a loss what to do in the matter, bethought himself to drive the rest of the cattle up to the cave. And when those within perceived the voice and scent of their fellows, they lowed in answer to those without, and their voice became 39.4. an accuser of the theft. Cacus, then, when he was caught in his crime, turned to defence and called upon those accustomed to keep the fields with him; but Heracles, beating him down with his club, slew him, and leading out the cattle, since he saw the place well suited for harbouring evildoers, threw down the cave upon it with his staff. And having purified the slaughter at the river, he set up near the place an altar of Zeus the Finder, which is in Rome beside the Triple gate, and sacrificed to the god one calf as a thank-offering for the finding of the cattle. This sacrifice the city of Rome still performed in my day, using in it all Greek customs, just as he established. 40.1. The Aborigines and those of the Arcadians who dwelt in the Pallantium, when they learned of the death of Cacus and saw Heracles, hating the one for his robberies but struck with awe at the look of the other, thought they beheld some divine being, and counted the loss of the robber a great piece of good fortune. The poorer among them, plucking branches of laurel, which grew abundantly about the place, wreathed both him and themselves; and their kings came to invite Heracles to a guest-feast. And when, as he related his name and race and deeds, they learned them, they put into his hands both their land and themselves in friendship. 40.2. But Evander, who had still earlier heard Themis declare that it was fated that Heracles, born of Zeus and Alcmene, should, exchanging his mortal nature, become immortal through virtue, as soon as he learned who he was, wishing to be the first of all men to propitiate Heracles with the honours of the gods, hastily set up an improvised altar and sacrificed at it an unyoked calf, having related the oracle to Heracles and asked him to begin the rites. 40.3. And Heracles, admiring the men for their hospitality, received the people with a feast, sacrificing some of the cattle and setting apart the tithes of the rest of the spoil; and the kings he presented with much land of the Ligurians and the other neighbouring peoples, the rule of which they greatly prized, having driven out of it certain lawless men. It is said besides that he made a request of the inhabitants—since they were the first to deem him a god—that they should preserve for him immortal honours, sacrificing an unyoked calf every year and performing the rite according to Greek usages; and that he taught them the sacrifices, so that they might ever offer what was pleasing to him, taking over two of the distinguished houses. 40.4. And those who then learned the Greek rite were the Potitii and the Pinarii, from whom the families long continued to have charge of the sacrifices, as he established—the Potitii leading the rite and beginning the burnt-offerings, and the Pinarii being excluded from a share of the entrails and holding the second honour in whatever else had to be done by both. And this dishonour, they say, was laid upon them on account of their late arrival, since, having been bidden to come at dawn, they arrived when the entrails of the victims had already been consumed. 40.5. Now, however, the charge of these rites no longer rests with these families, but slaves bought at public charge perform them. For what causes the custom was changed, and what manifestation of the divinity occurred concerning the change of the sacrificers, I shall relate when I come to that part of my 40.6. account. The altar on which Heracles offered the tithes is called by the Romans the Greatest, and is near the so-called Cattle Market, held sacred above any other by the inhabitants; for upon it oaths and compacts are made by those wishing to transact anything securely, and frequent tithings of goods are offered in fulfilment of vows. In construction, however, it falls far short of its repute. In many other parts of Italy too precincts have been dedicated to the god, and altars set up both in cities and along the roads; and one would rarely find a place in Italy where the god does not happen to be honoured. Such, then, is the legendary account handed down concerning him. 41.1. But the truer account, which many of those who have related his deeds in the form of history have followed, is this: that Heracles, having become the greatest general of his time and commanding a great force, traversed all the land within the Ocean, putting down whatever tyranny was harsh and grievous to its subjects, or city that insolently outraged its neighbours, or settlements of men using a savage way of life and lawless slaughter of strangers; and establishing lawful kingdoms and temperate governments and humane and sociable ways of life. Besides this, blending barbarians with Greeks and inlanders with sea-folk, who until then had held suspicious and intractable intercourse, founding cities in desolate lands, turning aside rivers that flooded the plains, cutting tracks through trackless mountains, and contriving all else, so that all land and sea should become common to the uses of all. 41.2. And he came into Italy not with a single ship nor merely driving a herd of cattle (for neither was the region in the path of those returning from Iberia to Argos, nor would it, for the mere passing through, have been deemed worthy of such honour), but leading a great army for the subjugation and rule of the men there, having already subdued Iberia; and he was compelled to spend more time there, both because of the absence of his fleet, which happened when winter set in, and because not all the peoples holding Italy came over to him willingly. 41.3. For besides the other barbarians, the Ligurian race, numerous and warlike, established at the passes of the Alpine mountains, undertook to bar his entrances into Italy by arms; where the greatest struggle befell the Greeks, all their missiles failing them in the battle. Aeschylus, among the ancient poets, makes this war plain in his Prometheus Unbound; for Prometheus is there represented as foretelling to Heracles, among other things, what was to befall him in each part of the expedition against Geryon, and in particular, concerning the Ligurian war, relating how the struggle would not be easy. The verses run thus: "You will come to the fearless host of the Ligurians, where, fierce though you are, you will not, I well know, find fault with the battle; for it is fated that even your missiles shall fail you there." 42.1. And when, having subdued these, he had gained control of the passes, some delivered their cities to him willingly—especially such as were of Greek race or had no forces worth reckoning—but the greater part submitted only after war and siege. 42.2. Among these conquered in battle, they say, was also the Cacus whom the Romans tell of in legend—a ruler altogether barbarous, lord of savage men, perched upon strong places and on that account troublesome to his neighbours. When he learned that Heracles had encamped in the adjoining plain, equipping himself after the manner of robbers, he made a sudden raid while the army slept and, gathering up such of the spoil as he came upon unguarded, 42.3. drove it off. Later, shut up in a siege by the Greeks, he both saw his strongholds taken by storm and was himself slain within his fastnesses. His strongholds being razed, the surrounding places were taken over by those who had come out with Heracles, each on their own account—certain Arcadians who were with Evander, and Faunus the king of the Aborigines. And one might conjecture that those of the Greeks who remained there—the Epeans and the Arcadians from Pheneus and the Trojans—were left behind for 42.4. the guarding of the country. For this too was one of the generalship-like deeds of Heracles, and as fit to be admired as any: that he led along on his campaigns, for a time, those uprooted from the conquered cities, but, when they had zealously helped him bear the wars through, settled them in lands won by the spear and enriched them with wealth furnished by others. For these things, then, the greatest name and glory of Heracles came to be in Italy, and not on account of the passage through, which had nothing august about it. 43.1. Some say that he also left behind in these regions, which the Romans now inhabit, sons born of two women: Pallas, by the daughter of Evander, whose name they say was Launa; and Latinus, by a certain Hyperborean girl, whom her father gave him as a hostage and whom he led along, and for a time kept pure of marriage, but, when he was sailing to Italy, falling in love, he got with child; and when he was about to set off for Argos, he gave her in marriage to Faunus the king of the Aborigines. For which reason the many believe Latinus to be the son of this man, not of Heracles. 43.2. Pallas, then, they say, died before reaching manhood; but Latinus, come to manhood, took over the rule of the Aborigines. And when he died without male children, in the battle against the neighbouring Rutulians, the rule passed to Aeneas the son of Anchises, who had become his son-in-law. But these things happened at other times. 44.1. Heracles, when he had settled all matters in Italy as he wished, and his naval force had come safely from Iberia, having sacrificed to the gods the tithes of the spoils and founded a small town named after himself, where his fleet lay at anchor—which even now, inhabited by the Romans, lies midway between Neapolis and Pompeii, having harbours secure in every season—and having obtained glory and emulation and honours equal to the gods among all who dwell in Italy, 44.2. set off for Sicily. And the guards and settlers of Italy left behind by him, established about the Saturnian hill, for a time were governed by themselves; but a little while later, having brought together their own way of life and laws and shrines of the gods with those of the Aborigines—as the Arcadians, and still earlier the Pelasgians, had done—and having shared the same city with the Aborigines, they came to be reckoned of the same race. Concerning the expedition of Heracles, then, and the remaining of the Peloponnesians in Italy, let this much be said. 44.3. In the second generation after the departure of Heracles, in about the fifty-fifth year, as the Romans themselves say, the king of the Aborigines was Latinus the son of Faunus, an offspring of Heracles, holding the rule in his thirty-fifth year. 45.1. About this time the Trojans who had escaped with Aeneas from Ilium, when the city was taken, put in at Laurentum, a shore of the Aborigines lying upon the Tyrrhenian Sea, not far from the mouth of the Tiber; and receiving from the Aborigines a place to dwell in and whatever else they asked, they built a town a little distance from the sea upon a certain hill, giving the city the name Lavinium. 45.2. A little later, changing their ancient name together with the Aborigines, they were named Latins after the king of the country; and removing from Lavinium in common with the inhabitants, they enclosed a larger city, which they called Alba, from which, setting out, they founded many other cities of those called the Prisci Latini, the greater part of which were still inhabited in my day. 45.3. Sixteen generations after the capture of Ilium, sending out a colony to the Pallantium and the Saturnia, where the Peloponnesians and Arcadians had made their first settlement, and where some embers of the ancient race still remained, they settled the places, enclosing the Pallantium with walls, so that it took the form of a city then for the first time. And they gave the foundation the name Rome, after Romulus, who had led out the colony, and who was the seventeenth 45.4. in descent from Aeneas. But concerning the coming of Aeneas into Italy too—since by some of the historians the account concerning him has been left unknown, and by others disputed—I wish to go through it not carelessly, comparing the histories both of the Greeks and of the Romans most to be trusted. What is said concerning him runs thus. 46.1. When Ilium was taken by the Achaeans—whether by the deceit of the wooden horse, as Homer has it, or by the treachery of the Antenoridae, or in some other way—the rest of the multitude in the city, Trojan and allied, being caught still in their beds, was slaughtered (for by night, it seems, the dread thing fell upon them unguarded); but Aeneas and the Trojans with him, allies present to the men of Ilium from the city of Dardanus and Ophrynium and the others who, while the lower city was being taken, contrived to gain perception of the danger, fleeing together to the strong parts of Pergamum, seized the citadel, guarded by a wall of its own, in which were both the ancestral shrines of the Trojans and the great wealth of treasure, as was natural in a stronghold, 46.2. and the best of the soldiery. There, holding out, they beat back those who tried to mount the height, and, running beneath through their familiarity with the lanes, took up the multitude that was slipping through amid the capture; and what escaped came to be more than what was taken. The enemy's immediate impulse—which they had, to make away with the whole city—and the failure to take the whole town at the first assault, Aeneas, having devised this stratagem, checked. And taking a reasonable calculation about the future—that it was an impossible thing to save a city of which the greater part was already in enemy hands—he bethought himself to yield the wall, emptied, to the enemy, but to save the persons themselves and the ancestral shrines and as much treasure as he could carry. 46.3. Having so resolved, he ordered the children and women and aged persons, and all others who needed a slow flight, to go out before from the city by the roads leading to Ida, while the Achaeans, eager to take the citadel, contrived nothing for the pursuit of the multitude slipping out of the city; and of the soldiery he posted part for the guarding of those going out, so that their flight might be safe and untoilsome, as far as was possible from the circumstances—and these were ordered to seize the strongest parts of Ida—while the rest, the best, he himself kept and held upon the wall, and made the flight less laborious for those who went out before, the enemy being engaged in the assault upon the wall. 46.4. But when Neoptolemus and those about him had mounted some part of the citadel, and all the Achaeans had come to their aid, he gave up the citadel, and, opening the gates, withdrew, keeping the rest of the fugitives in order, leading upon the strongest pairs of chariots his father and the ancestral gods and his wife and children and whatever else of greatest worth, whether person or treasure. 47.1. Meanwhile the Achaeans had taken the city by storm; and, intent upon the plundering, they allowed those fleeing much immunity to escape. And those about Aeneas, finding their own people still upon the road and all becoming one body, seized the strongest parts of Ida. 47.2. To them came those then dwelling in Dardanus, when they saw much flame, beyond what was usual, carried up from Ilium, having abandoned their city by night and left it desolate—save only such as, having equipped some naval force with Elymus and Aegestus, chanced to have gone out before from the city—and the whole people from the city of Ophrynium, and from the other Trojan cities all who clung to freedom; and this force, in the shortest time, became the greatest of the Trojan remnant. 47.3. Those, then, who had been saved with Aeneas from the capture, remaining in these regions, hoped before long to come down again to their own places when the enemy had sailed away; but the Achaeans, having enslaved the city and laid waste the neighbouring places and strongholds, were preparing to subdue 47.4. those in the mountains as well. When they had sent heralds about terms, asking them not to bring them to the necessity of war, the Trojans, assembling, made terms with them on these conditions: that Aeneas and those with him, carrying off whatever goods they had saved in their flight, should depart from the Troad within certain fixed times, delivering up the strongholds to the Achaeans; and that the Achaeans should furnish them safe-conduct out of all the land and sea over which they held sway, as they departed according to the agreement. 47.5. Aeneas, accepting these terms and thinking them the best in the circumstances, sent off Ascanius, the eldest of his sons, with a portion of the allied force, of which the greater part was Phrygian, to the land called Dascylitis, where is the Ascanian lake, having been summoned by the inhabitants to the kingship of the people; and Ascanius dwelt there for no long time. And when Scamandrius and the other Hectoridae, released from Greece by Neoptolemus, came to him, he restored them to their ancestral rule and came to Troy. 47.6. Concerning Ascanius, then, so much is told. As for Aeneas, taking the rest of his children and his father and the images of the gods, when his fleet had been made ready, he sailed across the Hellespont, making his voyage to the nearest peninsula, which lies before Europe and is called Pallene. A Thracian people held it, allies called Crusaeans, the most zealous of all who had joined them in the war. 48.1. The most trustworthy of the accounts concerning the flight of Aeneas, which Hellanicus, among the ancient historians, has used in his Trojan history, is this. But accounts not agreeing with this have been given by certain others concerning the same matters, which I for my part think less credible than this one. Let each of my hearers judge as he wishes. 48.2. Sophocles the tragic poet, in his play Laocoon, has represented Aeneas, when the city was about to be taken, removing to Ida, bidden by his father Anchises in remembrance of the things Aphrodite had enjoined, and from the signs lately occurring concerning the sons of Laocoon, having conjectured the coming destruction of the city. The iambic lines in it, spoken in the person of a messenger, run thus: "And now at the gates is Aeneas, the goddess's son, bearing his father upon his shoulders—down the thunder-stricken back drips a robe of fine linen—and round about all the whole household of his servants; and there throngs with him a multitude greater than you would think, who long for this colony of the Phrygians." 48.3. But Menecrates of Xanthus declares that he betrayed the city to the Achaeans because of his enmity toward Alexander, and that for this service the Achaeans permitted him to save his house. His account, beginning from the burial of Achilles, runs in this manner: "Distress held the Achaeans, and they thought the head of the army had been struck off. Nevertheless, having held a funeral feast for him, they made war with all their might, until Ilium fell, Aeneas giving it up. For Aeneas, being unhonoured by Alexander and excluded from his privileges, overthrew Priam; and having wrought these things, he had become one of the Achaeans." 48.4. Certain others say that he happened at that time to be tarrying at the Trojan naval station, others that he had been sent into Phrygia by Priam with a force on some military need; and there are those who make his departure more legendary. Let it stand as each man persuades himself. 49.1. The events after the departure provide the many with still more perplexity. For some, leading him as far as Thrace, say that he ended his life there—among whom are Cephalon of Gergis and Hegesippus, who wrote about Pallene, ancient men and worthy of note. Others, raising him up from Thrace, conduct him as far as Arcadia, and say that he dwelt in Arcadian Orchomenus, and in a place called Nesos (Island), although it lies inland, from the marshes and the river; and that what are called Capyae are a foundation of Aeneas and the Trojans, named Capyae after the Trojan Capys. These things are stated by, among others, Areithus 49.2. who wrote the Arcadian history. There are also those who tell in legend that Aeneas came hither, but that the end of his life did not befall him in these regions, but in Italy, as many others make plain, and Agathyllus the Arcadian, the poet, in an elegy, saying thus: "He came to Arcadia, and in Nesos he set down two daughters, born of the beds of Codone and Anthemone; but he himself sped to the Hesperian land, and begot a son, Romulus." 49.3. Of the coming of Aeneas and the Trojans into Italy, all the Romans are witnesses, and the things done by them in sacrifices and festivals are tokens of it, and the oracles of the Sibyl and the Pythian responses and many other things, which one would not despise as composed for the sake of plausibility. Many tokens too, clear down to the present time, remain among the Greeks, where they put in and among whom they made their stay on account of being unable to sail; of these, many as they are, I shall make the briefest mention I can. 49.4. First, coming to Thrace at the peninsula called Pallene, they put in. It was held, as I said, by barbarians called Crusaeans, who furnished them safe landings. Remaining there the winter season, they set up a temple of Aphrodite upon one of the headlands and founded a city, Aeneia, in which they left behind those unable through weariness to sail, and all who wished to remain there, as being thenceforth in their own land. This city endured until the Macedonian power that arose under the Successors of Alexander; and in the reign of Cassander it was demolished, when the city of Thessalonica was being founded, and the people of Aeneia, with many others, removed to the newly founded city. 50.1. Setting off from Pallene, the Trojans came to Delos, of which Anius was king; and there were many tokens in Delos of the coming of Aeneas and the Trojans, so long as the island flourished and was inhabited. Then, arriving at Cythera, another island that lies before the Peloponnese, 50.2. they set up a shrine of Aphrodite. And making their voyage from Cythera, when one of Aeneas's companions, Cinaethus, died not far from the Peloponnese, they buried him upon one of the headlands, which from him is now called Cinaethium; and renewing their kinship with the Arcadians—of which I shall speak in a later book—and tarrying a little while about these regions and leaving behind some of their number, they came to Zacynthus. 50.3. The Zacynthians too received them in friendship on account of kinship; for of Dardanus the son of Zeus and Electra the daughter of Atlas, they say, two sons were born from Bateia, Zacynthus and Erichthonius, of whom the latter was the ancestor of Aeneas, while Zacynthus was the founder of the island. In remembrance, then, of this kinship, and through the kindly disposition of the inhabitants, tarrying there and at the same time held back by being unable to sail, they offered to Aphrodite, at the shrine they had built, a sacrifice which the Zacynthians perform in common to this day; and they hold a contest for youths, of running among other contests; and the victory-prize the first to reach the temple receives. It is called the race of Aeneas and Aphrodite, and 50.4. wooden images of both of these stand there. From there, making their voyage on the open sea, they put in at Leucas, the place being still held by the Acarnanians. And here again they set up that shrine of Aphrodite which is now in the islet between the Dioryctus and the city, and is called of Aphrodite Aeneias. Setting off from there and coming to Actium, they anchored at the headland of the Ambracian gulf. And from there they came to the city of Ambracia, of which Ambrax the son of Dexamenus the son of Heracles was king; and they left behind in both places memorials of their coming—at Actium a shrine of Aphrodite Aeneias and, near it, of the Great Gods, which existed even in my day; and at Ambracia a shrine of the same goddess and a hero-shrine of Aeneas near the small theatre, in which there was also a small archaic wooden image said to be of Aeneas, and which those whom they call temple-attendants among them honoured with sacrifices. 51.1. From Ambracia, Anchises, with the ships, coasting along the land, put in at the harbour of Buthrotum in Epirus; while Aeneas and the most vigorous of the army with him, completing a two days' journey, came to Dodona to consult the god, and found there the Trojans who were with Helenus. Having taken up oracles concerning the colony and presented the god with Trojan offerings—among them bronze mixing-bowls, some of which still survive, declaring by very ancient inscriptions those who dedicated them—they came to the fleet, having completed a journey of about four days. The coming of the Trojans to Buthrotum is also made plain by a certain hill, which they then used as a camp, 51.2. called Troy. From Buthrotum, coasting along the land as far as the harbour then named after Anchises, but now having a less clear name, and setting up there too a shrine of Aphrodite, they crossed the Ionian Sea, having as guides of the voyage those who had sailed with them willingly, following along—the men with Patron of Thurii. And of these the greater part, when the army had come safely to Italy, returned home again; but Patron, persuaded by Aeneas to share in the colony, and with him some of his friends, remained in the expedition; and these, some say, settled in Alontium in Sicily. In remembrance of this service the Romans in time gave to the Acarnanians Leucas and Anactorium, taken from the Corinthians; permitted them, when they wished, to restore the Oeniadae; and gave them the Echinades islands to enjoy in common with the Aetolians. 51.3. Those with Aeneas made their landing not at one place in Italy, but, with the greater part of the ships, anchored at the promontory of Iapygia, then called Salentinus, and with the rest at the place called Athenaeum, where Aeneas himself chanced to set foot in Italy (this place is a headland, and upon it a summer anchorage, which from that time is called the harbour of Aphrodite); and they coasted along as far as the strait, keeping Italy at hand, leaving behind in these places too certain traces of their coming—among others a bronze bowl in the shrine of Hera, declaring by an ancient inscription the name of Aeneas, who presented it to the goddess. 52.1. Coming off Sicily—whether resolving of purpose to put in there, or forced by foul winds, such as are wont to occur about this sea—they put in at the part of the island about the place called Drepana. There they fell in with those who had gone out before from Troy with Elymus and Aegestus, who, having found fortune and a favouring wind, and at the same time weighed down by no great baggage, had in a short time come down to Sicily and settled about a river called Crimisus in the land of the Sicani, receiving the place from them in friendship on account of the kinship of Aegestus, who had been born and reared in Sicily through 52.2. some such circumstance as this. One of his ancestors, a distinguished man of the Trojan race, became at variance with Laomedon; and the king, taking him on some charge, slew him and all his male offspring, for fear of suffering something at their hands; but the daughters, being still maidens, he thought it not seemly to kill, yet not safe to suffer to dwell among the Trojans; so he gave them to merchants, bidding them carry them off as far away as possible. 52.3. With these, as they departed, there sailed a youth of the distinguished class, overcome with love of one of them, and he married the girl when she had been brought to Sicily; and to them, while they tarried among the Sicels, was born a son named Aegestus, who, learning the manners and tongue of the inhabitants, when it befell that his parents died, while Priam reigned in Troy, contrived to have his return granted him; and having helped bear through the war against the Achaeans, when the city was being taken, he sailed back again to Sicily, making his flight with Elymus in three ships, which Achilles, when he was plundering the Trojan cities, had lost when they fell upon sunken reefs. 52.4. Falling in, then, with the men aforesaid, Aeneas treated them kindly and built them cities, Aegesta and Elyma, and left behind in the towns even a portion of his own army—as I conjecture, of his own free purpose, that there might be safe resting-places and harbours for those weighed down by weariness or otherwise oppressed by the sea; but, as some write, his fleet having been diminished by the burning which certain of the women, oppressed by the wandering, brought about, he of necessity left behind the multitude no longer able to sail with him, from the burnt ships. 53.1. Of the coming of Aeneas and the Trojans to the Sicels there are many other proofs, but the most conspicuous are the altar of Aphrodite Aeneias set up upon the summit of Elymus, and a shrine of Aeneas set up at Aegesta—the one built by Aeneas himself to his mother, the shrine made a dedication by those left behind from the expedition in memory of him who had saved them. The Trojan element with Elymus and Aegestus, then, remained in these places, and continued to be called Elymi. For Elymus held precedence in dignity, being of the royal race, 53.2. from whom the whole took its name. Those who sailed with Aeneas from Sicily through the Tyrrhenian Sea first anchored at the part of Italy by the harbour of Palinurus, which is said to have obtained this name from one of Aeneas's helmsmen who died there. Then they touched at an island, to which they gave the name Leucasia, from a woman, a cousin of Aeneas, who died about this place. 53.3. From there, putting in at a deep and fair harbour among the Opicans, when there too Misenus, one of the distinguished men, died, they named the harbour after him; and putting in by chance at the island Prochyta and the headland Caieta, they likewise gave names to the places—women having died there, wishing to make the places memorials. Of these, the one is said to have been a kinswoman of Aeneas, the other a nurse. At last they came to Laurentum in Italy, where, ceasing from their wandering, they pitched a palisade; and the place in which they encamped is from that time called Troy, and is distant from the sea about four stades. 53.4. I have written these things and made this digression for necessity's sake, since of the historians some say that Aeneas did not even come to Italy with the Trojans; others, that it was a different Aeneas, not the one born of Aphrodite and Anchises; others, Ascanius the son of Aeneas; others, certain others. And there are those who say that the Aeneas born of Aphrodite, having established the colony in Italy, was conveyed back home again and reigned over Troy, and at his death left the kingdom to Ascanius his son, and that his line long held the rule—being, as I conjecture, misled by the verses of Homer wrongly taken. 53.5. For Poseidon is represented by him in the Iliad foretelling the coming distinction of Aeneas and of those to be born of him, somewhat thus: "And now indeed shall the might of Aeneas rule over the Trojans, and his children's children, who shall be born hereafter." Supposing, then, that Homer knew the men to be holding sway in Phrygia, and that it was not possible for those dwelling in Italy to reign over the Trojans, they invented the return of Aeneas. But it was not impossible for him to rule over the Trojans he led along, though governed elsewhere; and one might find other causes of the error as well. 54.1. But if any are troubled by the fact that tombs of Aeneas are spoken of and shown in many places, since it is impossible that the same man should have been buried in several places, let them, reflecting that this perplexity is common in the case of many men—and especially of those who have had illustrious fortunes but wandering lives—learn that there was one place that received their bodies, but that memorials were built among many through the goodwill of those who had received some benefits through them, especially if some of their race survived, or there was a foundation of some city, or some lasting and kindly sojourns; such as we know are told in legend also concerning 54.2. this hero. For to Ilium having granted that it was not utterly destroyed at its capture; to what is called Bebrycia having contrived that the auxiliary force was saved; in Phrygia having left his son Ascanius as king; in Pallene having founded a city named after himself; in Arcadia having given his daughters in marriage; in Sicily having left a part of his army; and in many other places seeming to have bestowed kindly sojourns—he had their goodwill freely given, on account of which, when he had left the life among men, he was honoured with hero-shrines and the building of memorials in many places. 54.3. For come, what causes could one suppose for his memorials in Italy, if he neither ruled these regions nor made sojourns in them nor was known to them at all? But concerning these things it shall be said again hereafter, as the account on each occasion requires it to be made plain. 55.1. That the Trojan fleet sailed no farther into Europe was caused both by the oracles, which found their fulfilment in these regions, and by the divine power, in many ways indicating its own will. For when, using Laurentum as an anchorage, they had pitched their tents about the shore, first, when the men were pressed by thirst, the place having no water (I tell what I received from the inhabitants), springs of sweetest water were seen rising of themselves from the earth, from which the whole army watered itself, and the place became encompassed with water, the stream running down from the springs to the sea. 55.2. Now, however, the springs no longer well up so as even to overflow, but there is a little water gathered in a hollow place, called by the inhabitants the shrine of the sun; and two altars are shown beside it, the one turned toward the rising, the other toward the setting of the sun, Trojan foundations, at which they tell in legend that Aeneas offered the first sacrifice to the god as a thank-offering for the waters. 55.3. Then, as they were taking their meal upon the ground, parsley had been strewn beneath the food for many, and this served as a kind of table for the viands; but, as some say, it was cakes made of wheaten meal, for cleanliness in the eating. When the food set out had been consumed, one and then another ate of the parsley, or cakes, strewn beneath them; and thereupon one of them happened to say—whether one of Aeneas's sons, as the story has it, or one of his tent-fellows—"But now indeed we have eaten even the table." And when they heard this, all raised a shout, that the first part of the prophecy now had 55.4. its fulfilment for them. For there was an oracle of theirs—as some say, given at Dodona, but as others write, in the red mainland of Ida, where dwelt a Sibyl, a native nymph who uttered prophecies—who told them to sail toward the setting of the sun until they should come to the place in which they would eat their tables; and when they should perceive this happen, to make a four-footed creature their guide, and where the 55.5. animal should grow weary, there to build a city. Calling to mind, then, this oracle, some, at Aeneas's bidding, carried the images of the gods from the ship to the appointed place, others built bases and altars for them, while the women, with ritual cries and dances, escorted the sacred objects, and those about Aeneas, the sacrifice having been made ready, stood about the altar with their garlands. 56.1. While they were making their vows, the sow that was about to be consecrated, being pregnant and not far from its time, when the sacrificers began the rites, shook itself loose, escaped those holding it, and ran up the country. Aeneas, understanding that this was the four-footed creature whom the oracle declared to be their guide, followed it with a few men, keeping a little behind, fearing lest, by the tumult of the pursuers, it should be turned aside from the path appointed 56.2. by the divinity. And the sow, having gone about four-and-twenty stades from the sea, ran up a certain hill, where, worn out with weariness, it sat down. To Aeneas (for the prophecies seemed to have their fulfilment), seeing the place to be neither in fair land nor near the sea, and not even that affording good anchorage, much perplexity came on, whether he ought, in obedience to the oracle, to settle there, where they would spend forever a grievous life, enjoying nothing good, or should go farther in search of better land. 56.3. While he was pondering these things and holding the gods to blame, suddenly, it is said, a voice from the glen, the speaker being unseen, fell upon him, bidding him remain there and build a city quickly, and not, yielding to the perplexity of his present opinion—because he was not to fix his life in a land good for pasture—push away the prosperity that 56.4. was to come, and all but present. For it was fated for him, setting out from this grievous and small dwelling at first, to gain much good land in time; and to his children and descendants there should belong an empire the greatest and longest-lasting. This, then, should for the present be a resting-place for the Trojans; but after as many years as the sow should bear young, another city, prosperous and great, should be founded by those born of him. And Aeneas, hearing this and deeming the matter of the voice to be something divine, did as the god commanded. 56.5. But others say that, while the man was in distress and his body unstrung with grief, having neither gone down to the camp nor taken food, but bivouacked there as chance had it that night, there stood over him in a dream a great and marvellous vision, likened to one of the ancestral gods, suggesting the things said a little before; but in which way the truth lies would be known to the gods. The next day the sow is said to have borne thirty young, and after as many years another city was founded by the Trojans according to the oracle, of which I shall speak in its proper place. 57.1. Aeneas sacrificed the sow's offspring, together with the dam, to the ancestral gods in this place, where the shrine now is, and which the Lavinians, keeping it inaccessible to others, hold sacred. Bidding the Trojans shift their camp to the hill, he set up the images of the gods in the strongest part, and at once with all zeal set about the building of the town, going down and taking from the surrounding places whatever was useful to him for the building, and especially what was likely to prove grievous to those deprived of it—iron and timber and the implements of husbandry. 57.2. To Latinus, who was then king, warring against a neighbouring people called the Rutulians and faring ill in his battles, the events were reported in their most fearful aspect: that all his seaboard was being made desolate by a foreign army, and that, if he should not quickly check what was being done, the war against his neighbours would prove to him but gold. Hearing this, fear came upon the man, and at once abandoning the present war, he marched against the Trojans with a great army. 57.3. But seeing them armed as Greeks and holding their ground in fair order, awaiting the danger undismayed, he turned aside from the immediate hazard—the intention he had had, setting out from home, of overcoming them at the first assault—as one who could no longer do so; and encamping upon a certain hill, he thought he ought first to recover his force from the present fatigue, which had been great for them, from the long march and the strenuous pursuit. 57.4. Bivouacking there through the night, he formed the resolve to engage the enemy at the beginning of dawn. But when he had resolved this, a native divinity, standing over him in his sleep, bade him receive the Greeks as fellow-dwellers in the land; for they had come as a great benefit to Latinus and a common good to the Aborigines. And to Aeneas the ancestral gods, appearing the same night, urged him to persuade Latinus to grant them willingly the dwelling in whatever place they wished, and to use the Greek force as an ally rather than an adversary; and the dream forbade both to begin the battle. When day came, and the forces were drawn up for battle, heralds came to the leaders from both sides asking the same thing, that they should come together for a parley; and this came to pass. 58.1. First Latinus, making complaint of the sudden and undeclared war, asked Aeneas to say who he was and with what purpose he was plundering the country, having suffered no harm beforehand, and not unaware that everyone who is first wronged defends himself against the one who begins a war; whereas everything would have been granted him, if he asked anything reasonable, in friendship and from willing inhabitants—but, passing over the common justice of all men, he had thought it right, more shamefully than honourably, to take the same things by force. 58.2. When he had spoken thus, Aeneas answered: "We are by race Trojans, and we were of a city not the least illustrious among the Greeks; deprived of it by the Achaeans, subdued in a ten years' war, we wander about as exiles in need of a city and a land in which to dwell henceforth, and, in obedience to the commands of the gods, have come hither; and to us, as the oracles declare, this land alone is left as a harbour from our wandering. We provide ourselves from the country with what we need, more in misfortune than in seemliness, though we lately wished to do so as pleasantly as possible. 58.3. But we will requite these things with many good returns of service, furnishing to you both bodies and souls well trained to meet dangers, to use as you wish—keeping your land unravaged, and zealously helping you win that of your enemies. And we make this petition of you, not to take what has been done in anger, considering that we did these things not out of insolence but forced by necessity; and all that is involuntary is to be pardoned. 58.4. And it behoves you to resolve nothing hostile concerning us who hold out our hands; but if you do, we shall entreat the gods and divinities who hold this land to be merciful to us, and shall try to defend ourselves against you who begin the war, even for the things we do under compulsion. For this would not be the first nor the greatest war we have had to endure." 58.5. When Latinus heard this, he answered him: "Indeed, I have goodwill toward the whole Greek race, and I am very grieved at the necessary misfortunes of men, and I should set great store by your being saved, if it were made plain to me that you have come in need of a dwelling, and will be content with a sufficient portion of land, and will share in what is given in friendship, but not take away my dominion by force. But if this account of yours is true, I think it right to give and receive pledges of these things, which will keep our agreements free from guile." 59.1. Aeneas approving what was said, there were made between the peoples, upon oaths, compacts such as these: that the Aborigines should give the Trojans as much land as they asked, about forty stades in every direction as one went out from the hill; and that the Trojans should help the Aborigines in the war at hand, and join in campaigns wherever else they were summoned; and that both in common should do their utmost on each other's behalf, both with hand and with counsel. 59.2. Having so agreed, and confirmed their pledges by the giving of children as hostages, they marched in common against the cities of the Rutulians; and having in a short time subdued all matters there, they came to the Trojan town, still half-finished, and all using one zeal, walled it. 59.3. Aeneas gave the foundation the name Lavinium, as the Romans themselves say, from the daughter of Latinus, whose name they say was Launa; but, as some others of the Greek writers of legend have said, from the daughter of Anius the king of the Delians, who was likewise named Launa, and who, dying of disease during the first settlement of the city, and being buried in the place where she had fallen ill, became its memorial. She is said to have sailed with the Trojans, having been given by her father to Aeneas at his request, being prophetic and wise. 59.4. It is said that during the building of Lavinium signs such as these occurred to the Trojans: a fire having of itself blazed up out of the glen, a wolf was carrying dry wood in its mouth and throwing it upon the fire, while an eagle, flying near, fanned the flame with the beating of its wings; but, contriving the contrary to these, a fox, bringing its tail soaked from the river, beat at the burning fire; and now those who were kindling prevailed, now the one wishing to put it out; but at last the two prevailed, and the other went off, no longer able to do anything. 59.5. Aeneas, seeing this, said that the colony would be illustrious and marvellous and would come to the greatest renown, but, as it grew, an object of envy to its neighbours and grievous to them; yet it would nevertheless prevail over those opposing it, having received from the divine a fortune stronger than the envy of men that would oppose it. Such, then, are said to have been the conspicuous tokens that occurred of what was to befall the city; and there are memorials of them in the marketplace of the Lavinians, bronze images of the animals preserved from very ancient time. 60.1. When the city had been built for the Trojans, a strong desire came upon all to enjoy what was useful from one another; and their kings first began, mingling the dignity of the native and the foreign race by the bond of marriage, Latinus giving his daughter Launa to Aeneas as wife. 60.2. Then the others too, taking the same desire as their kings, and in a very short time bringing together their customs and laws and shrines of the gods, joining in marriage with one another and blended in the partnership of wars—all together, calling themselves by one common name, Latins, after the king of the Aborigines—so firmly remained by their agreements that no time thereafter parted them from one another. 60.3. The peoples, then, that came together and shared their lives, from whom the Roman race is sprung, before the city they now have was founded, are these: first the Aborigines, who drove the Sicels out of these regions, Greeks of old from the Peloponnese, of those who with Oenotrus removed their dwelling from what is now called Arcadia, as I am persuaded; next the Pelasgians, who migrated from the land then called Haemonia, but now Thessaly; third, those who came with Evander into Italy from the city of Pallantium; after these, of the Peloponnesians who campaigned with Heracles, the Epeans and Pheneatae, with whom some Trojan element too is mingled; and last, the Trojans who were saved with Aeneas from Ilium and Dardanus and the other Trojan cities. 61.1. That the Trojan people too was Greek in the highest degree, having once set out from the Peloponnese, has been stated long ago by certain others, and shall be told by me too in a few words. The account concerning them runs thus. Atlas became the first king in what is now called Arcadia, and dwelt about the mountain called Cauconium. He had seven daughters, now said to have been set in the heavens under the name of the Pleiades, of whom Zeus married one, Electra, and 61.2. begot of her sons, Iasus and Dardanus. Iasus, then, remained unmarried, but Dardanus took to wife Chryse the daughter of Pallas, of whom were born to him sons, Idaeus and Deimas. These for a time, having received the dominion of Atlas, reigned in Arcadia; then, a great flood having come about Arcadia, the plains were turned into marsh and for a long time could not be tilled, and the men (for they dwelt up in the mountains, providing their food scantily), perceiving that the remaining land would not be sufficient to nourish all, divided themselves in two; and of them some remained in Arcadia, setting up as king Deimas the son of Dardanus, while the rest 61.3. set out from the Peloponnese with a great expedition. Making their voyage along Europe, they came to the gulf called the Black, and chanced to anchor at a certain island of Thrace, of which I cannot say whether it was inhabited before, or desolate; to it they gave a name compounded of a man and a place, Samothrace—for the place was of Thrace, and the founder was Samon, son of Hermes and of a Cyllenian nymph named Rhene. 61.4. There, having tarried no long time, since life was not easy for them, contending with a grievous land and a savage sea, leaving a few in the island, the greater part set out again into Asia, having Dardanus as leader of the colony; for Iasus, in the island, was slain by a thunderbolt, reaching for the bed of Demeter. And making their landing at what is now called the Hellespont, they settled about the land afterward called Phrygia—Idaeus the son of Dardanus, holding a part of the host, in the mountains which from him are now called the Idaean, where, having set up a shrine of the Mother of the gods, he established the orgies and mysteries which down to the present time endure throughout all Phrygia; and Dardanus, in what is now called the Troad, built a city of the same name as himself, Teucer the king having given him the places, from whom the land was anciently called Teucris. 61.5. This Teucer, many others and Phanodemus who wrote the Attic antiquities say, removed from Attica into Asia, being ruler of the deme of Xypete, and they offer many proofs of the account. Having gained control of much good land, holding no great native population, Teucer gladly saw Dardanus and the Greek element that came with him, both for the sake of an alliance in the wars against the barbarians, and that the land might not be desolate. 62.1. The account requires that I relate also from whom Aeneas was sprung; and this too I shall make plain in brief. Dardanus, when it befell that Chryse the daughter of Pallas, of whom his former sons were born to him, died, married Bateia the daughter of Teucer; and there was born to him a son, Erichthonius, who is said to have become the most prosperous of all men, having inherited both his father's rule and that which had been under his maternal grandfather. 62.2. Of Erichthonius and Callirrhoe the daughter of Scamander was born Tros, from whom the people has its name; of Tros and Acallaris the daughter of Eumedes was Assaracus; of him and Clytodora the daughter of Laomedon, Capys; of Capys and a Naiad nymph, Hieromneme, Anchises; of Anchises and Aphrodite, Aeneas. That the Trojan race too was Greek from the first has thus been made plain by me. 63.1. Concerning the times in which Lavinium was founded, different writers say different things; to me, however, those who place it in the second year after the departure from Troy seem to speak the more probably. For Ilium was taken when the summer was now ending, seventeen days before the summer solstice, on the eighth day from the end of the month Thargelion, as the Athenians reckon the times; and there were twenty days left over to complete that year after the solstice. In the seven-and-thirty days, then, that elapsed from the capture, I think the Achaeans both ordered the affairs about the city, and received the embassies from those who had revolted, and made oaths with them; 63.2. and in the next year, the first after the capture, about the autumn equinox, the Trojans, setting out from the land, crossed the Hellespont, and putting in at Thrace, tarried there the winter season, receiving those who came in from the flight and preparing for the voyage out. Setting out from Thrace at the beginning of spring, they completed the intervening voyage as far as Sicily; and there, when they had anchored, that year ended, and they spent the second winter founding the cities with the Elymi in Sicily. 63.3. When sailing was possible, setting out from the island, they crossed the Tyrrhenian Sea and at last came to Laurentum, the shore of the Aborigines, in the middle of summer. Receiving the place, they founded Lavinium in it, completing the second year from the capture. Concerning these things, then, what opinion I hold has been made plain by me. 64.1. Aeneas, having furnished the city sufficiently with shrines and the other adornments, of which the greater part still existed in my day, in the next year, the third from the departure, reigned over the Trojans alone; and in the fourth, Latinus having died, he took over his kingdom as well, both through the bond of kinship with him—Launa having become heiress after the death of Latinus—and for the sake of the generalship in the war against the neighbours. 64.2. For the Rutulians again revolted from Latinus, taking as leader one of the deserters, a kinsman of Latinus's wife Amita, named Tyrrhenus. This man, blaming his connexion concerning the marriage of Launa, because, passing over the kinship, he had allied himself to strangers—Amita inciting him and certain others assisting—leading the force which he himself commanded, joined the Rutulians. 64.3. War having arisen from these charges, and a strong battle, both Latinus and Tyrrhenus and many of the others died; but those with Aeneas nevertheless prevailed. After this Aeneas took over the rule that had been under his father-in-law. And having reigned three years after the death of Latinus, in the fourth he died in war. 64.4. For the Rutulians from the cities all marched against him, and with them Mezentius the king of the Tyrrhenians, fearing for his own country; for, seeing the Greek power already advancing to greatness, he was vexed. A strong battle having occurred not far from Lavinium, and many having perished on both sides, the armies were parted when night came on; but the body of Aeneas, nowhere appearing, some conjectured to have passed over to the gods, others to have perished in the river beside which the battle took place. 64.5. And the Latins built him a hero-shrine, adorned with this inscription: "To the father, a god of the underworld, who governs the stream of the river Numicius." But there are those who say it was built by Aeneas to Anchises, who died the year before this war. It is a small mound, and round about it trees planted in rows, worth seeing. 65.1. About the seventh year after the capture of Ilium, when Aeneas had departed from among men, Euryleon—he who had been renamed Ascanius in the flight—took over the leadership of the Latins. The Trojans were at this time shut up within their walls, and to the enemy a force was ever coming on, while that of the Latins was unable to aid those besieged in Lavinium. 65.2. At first those about Ascanius invited the enemy to friendship and reasonable terms; but when they paid no heed to them, they were compelled to leave it to them to compose the war on whatever conditions they themselves should judge fitting. But when the king of the Tyrrhenians laid upon them, among other intolerable demands as upon men enslaved, that they should carry off to the Tyrrhenians every year as much wine as the land of the Latins should bear, deeming the thing not to be endured, they voted that the fruit of the vine should be sacred to Zeus, Ascanius declaring the proposal; and, exhorting one another to be zealous combatants and entreating the gods to assist them in the venture, they went out of the city, having watched for a moonless night. 65.3. And straightway falling upon the enemy's palisade, which lay nearest the city and was a bulwark of the rest of the force—built in a strong place and holding the best youth of the Tyrrhenians, of whom the son of Mezentius, by name Lausus, was the leader—no one foreseeing the assault, they easily took the stronghold. While this place was being taken, those encamped in the plains, seeing the untimely light and hearing the cries of the perishing, fled, abandoning the level places, to the 65.4. mountains. In this there was much confusion and tumult, as is natural when an army moves by night, expecting the enemy to fall upon them at any moment, making their march in no order nor by divisions. And the Latins, since they had taken the fort by assault and learned that the rest of the army was thrown into confusion, pressed upon them, slaying and pursuing. Of the enemy, not only did no one attempt to turn to defence, but no one could even learn in what evils they were; and through tumult and helplessness, some, being carried over cliffs, perished, others, falling into ravines without outlet, were taken, and the greater part, not recognizing one another in the dark, treated each other as enemies, and the greatest destruction among them was self-inflicted slaughter. And Mezentius, seizing a certain hill with a few men, when he learned of his son's death and how great an army of his had been destroyed and in what a place he had shut himself up, 65.5. being in want of supplies, sent heralds to Lavinium to treat of friendship; and Ascanius advising the Latins to husband their fortune, he obtained safe-conduct, departed under truce with all the force he had, and for all the time thereafter, having dissolved his enmity toward the Latins, was a steadfast friend. 66.1. Thirty years after the founding of Lavinium, Ascanius the son of Aeneas, in accordance with the oracle given to Aeneas, founded another city, and transferred to the newly founded one those from Lavinium and such of the other Latins as wished to dwell better, giving the city the name Alba. Alba, in the Greek tongue, is "White"; but for the sake of distinction it is marked off from another city of the same name by an additional epithet describing its shape, and the name is now as it were compounded from both, Alba Longa—that is, "White Long." 66.2. Now indeed it is desolate; for in the reign of Tullus Hostilius king of the Romans, having seemed to be at variance with the colony over the supremacy, it was destroyed; and the multitude dwelling in it, Rome, which had demolished the mother-city, received. But these things happened in the proper times; while it was being settled, it was built beside a mountain and a lake, occupying the space between both, and these were as it were walls of the city, making it hard to take. For the mountain is among the very strong and lofty, and the lake deep and great, and the plain receives it through sluices that are opened, the men husbanding the water as much as they wish. 66.3. Below the city lie plains marvellous to behold, and rich to bring forth wines and fruits of every kind, in no way inferior to the rest of Italy, but especially what is called the Alban wine, sweet and fine—save the so-called Falernian, the most excellent of all the rest. 67.1. In the founding of the city the greatest marvel is said to have occurred. A temple having been built for the images of the gods which Aeneas had brought from the Troad and set up in Lavinium—a temple having an inaccessible place—and the images having been conveyed from Lavinium into this inner sanctuary, on the following night, the doors being most carefully shut and neither the enclosures nor the roofs suffering anything, the images, having changed their station, were found lying upon their 67.2. ancient pedestals; and being conveyed again from Lavinium, with supplications and propitiatory sacrifices, into the same place, they likewise went back up. The men for a time were at a loss what to do in the matter, thinking it right neither to dwell apart from the ancestral gods nor to return again to the dwelling they had abandoned; but at last they found a resolution that was to suffice for both: to let the images remain in their place, but to bring back men from Alba to Lavinium to have charge of them as settlers. And those sent were six hundred, who removed with their households as keepers of the sacred things; and a leader was set over them, Aegestus. 67.3. These gods the Romans call Penates; and those who interpret the name into the Greek tongue, some declare them to be "Ancestral," others "Of Birth," some "Of Possession," others "Of the Inner Chamber," others "Of the Enclosure." Each of these seems to make the appellation according to some one of the things befalling them, and all are likely, in one way or another, to mean the same 67.4. thing. Concerning their shape and form Timaeus the historian declares thus: that the sacred objects lying in the inner shrines at Lavinium are iron and bronze heralds' wands and Trojan pottery; and that he himself learned these things from the inhabitants. But for my part, whatever it is not lawful for all to see, I think I ought neither to hear of from those who see it nor to write down; and I am indignant at others too, as many as think it right to seek out or to know more than is permitted by the law. 68.1. But what I myself know from having seen it, and which no fear forbids me to write about, is this. A temple is shown in Rome not far from the forum, along the short road leading to the Carinae, set in a dark recess, not great. The place is called in the native tongue "Of the Olive." In it lie images of the Trojan gods, which it is lawful for all to see, bearing an inscription declaring them the Penates. 68.2. They are two youths seated, holding spears, works of the ancient art. Many other images of these gods too we have beheld in ancient shrines, and in all of them appear two young men in military attire. It is permitted, then, to see these; but to hear and write about them, what Callistratus, who composed the work on Samothrace, relates, and Satyrus, who collected the ancient legends, and many others—the most ancient poet of whom we know being Arctinus. 68.3. They say, then, thus: that Chryse the daughter of Pallas, married to Dardanus, brought as her dowry the gifts of Athena, both the Palladia and the sacred objects of the Great Gods, having been taught their mysteries. And when the Arcadians, fleeing the flood, left the Peloponnese and fixed their lives in the Thracian island, Dardanus there built a shrine of these gods, keeping their proper names unspoken to others, and performed for them the mysteries which down to the present time are celebrated by the Samothracians. 68.4. And when he was leading the greater part of the people into Asia, he left the sacred objects of the gods and the mysteries to those who remained in the island; but the Palladia and the images of the gods, having had them made, he led with him. And consulting the oracle about his dwelling, he learned other things and received this oracle concerning the guarding of the sacred objects: "In the city you build set up an imperishable reverence ever to the gods, and reverence them with guardings, with sacrifices, and with dances. For so long as these august gifts of the daughter of Zeus remain in your land, given to your wife, your city shall be unsacked for all time, all your days." 69.1. Dardanus, then, left the images in the city founded by himself and called by a like name; but when Ilium was afterward settled, the sacred objects were conveyed there by his descendants. And the people of Ilium built for them a temple and an inner shrine upon the citadel, and guarded them with all the care they could, holding them to be heaven-sent and the masters of the city's safety. 69.2. And when the lower city was being taken, Aeneas, having become master of the citadel, taking up from the inner shrines the sacred objects of the Great Gods and the Palladium that still remained (for the other one, they say, Odysseus and Diomedes, coming to Ilium by night, took by theft), went off carrying them from the city and came leading them into Italy. 69.3. But Arctinus says that one Palladium was given by Zeus to Dardanus, and that this was in Ilium, hidden in an inaccessible place, while the city was being taken; and that an image of it, made so as to differ in nothing from the original, was set in the open for the deceiving of those who plotted against it, and that this the Achaeans, having plotted, took. 69.4. The sacred objects conveyed into Italy by Aeneas, then—trusting the men aforesaid, I write that they are the images of the Great Gods, whom the Samothracians, most of the Greeks, worship in mysteries, and the famed Palladium, which they say the sacred virgins guard, lying in the temple of Hestia, where also the immortal fire is preserved; concerning which it shall be told in a later book. There may be, besides these, other things unknown to us, the profane. And concerning the Trojan sacred objects let this much be said. 70.1. When Ascanius died in the thirty-eighth year of his reign, Silvius took over the leadership, brother of Ascanius, born after the death of Aeneas of Launa the daughter of Latinus, whom they say was reared in the mountains by the herdsmen. 70.2. For when Ascanius took over the kingdom, Launa, fearful that she might suffer some harm from him in the character of stepmother, being pregnant, gave herself to a certain Tyrrhenus, the overseer of the royal swine-herds, whom she knew to have been among the most familiar with Latinus. He, leading her into desolate woods, as though one of the ordinary women, guarding against being seen by those who knew her, reared her in the glen, having built a dwelling known to few; and the child being born, he took it up and reared it, naming it Silvius from the wood, as one might say in the Greek tongue "Hylaeus." 70.3. As time went on, when he perceived that much search for the woman was being made by the Latins, and that Ascanius was held in blame by the multitude as having made away with the girl, he declared the matter to the people and brought the woman with the child out of the glen. Having met, then, with such a fortune, Silvius had the aforesaid name, and all his line from him; and he took over the kingdom, when it befell that his brother died, the succession being disputed against one of the sons of Ascanius, Iulus, who, being the elder, thought it right to succeed to his father's rule. 70.4. But the people gave judgment, induced by other arguments and not least because Silvius was of a mother who was heiress of the rule. To Iulus, in place of the kingdom, a certain sacred authority and honour was added, surpassing the monarchy in freedom from danger and in ease of life, which his line enjoyed even down to my time, being called Iulii after him. And this became the greatest and at once the most illustrious of the houses of which we know, and brought forth men most excellent among leaders, to whom their virtues caused their nobility not to be disbelieved; concerning whom what is fitting shall be made plain in another book. 71.1. When Silvius had held the rule nine-and-twenty years, Aeneas his son, succeeding to the power, reigned one-and-thirty years. After him Latinus ruled fifty-one years. After him Alba nine-and-thirty years. After Alba, Capetus six-and-twenty. Then Capys eight-and-twenty. After Capys, Calpetus held the rule for thirteen years. 71.2. Next Tiberinus reigned eight years. He is said to have died in a battle that took place beside a river; and being carried away by the stream, he left the river named after himself, called before Albula. The successor of Tiberinus, Agrippa, reigned one-and-forty years. 71.3. After Agrippa, Allodius, a tyrannical thing and hateful to the gods, nineteen years; he, despising the divine powers, contrived imitations of thunderbolts and crashes resembling thunder, with which he thought fit to terrify men as a god. But when rains and thunderbolts fell upon his house, and the lake beside which he chanced to dwell took an unwonted flood, he was overwhelmed with his whole household and perished. And even now, when the lake shines clear in a certain part, whenever the water subsides and the depth grows still, ruins of colonnades and other traces of a dwelling appear. 71.4. Aventinus, succeeding to the power from him—from whom one of the seven hills built up together with Rome took its name—held the rule seven-and-thirty years. Procas after him three-and-twenty years. Then Amulius, holding the kingdom not with justice, which belonged to Numitor, who was his elder brother, ruled two-and-forty years. 71.5. And when Amulius was slain by Romulus and Remus, born of the sacred maiden, as shall presently be told, after his death Numitor, the maternal grandfather of the young men, recovered his lawful power. In the year following the beginning of Numitor's rule, the four hundred and thirty-second after the capture of Ilium, the Albans sending out a colony, Romulus and Remus holding the leadership of it, founded Rome, in the first year of the seventh Olympiad, in which Daïcles of Messene won the stade-race, Charops being archon at Athens, the first year of his ten-year term. 72.1. Since there is much dispute both about the time of the founding and about the founders of the city, I myself thought I ought not, as if these things were agreed by all, to pass over them in haste. For Cephalon of Gergis, a very ancient historian, says that the city was founded in the second generation after the Trojan War by those saved from Ilium with Aeneas, and declares its founder to be the one who led the colony, Romus, and that this man was one of the sons of Aeneas; and he says that Aeneas had four sons, Ascanius, Euryleon, Romulus, Romus. The same time and the same leader of the colony are stated by Demagoras and Agathyllus and many others. 72.2. But he who collected the priestesses at Argos and the things done in the term of each says that Aeneas, coming from the Molossians into Italy with Odysseus, became the founder of the city, and named it after one of the Trojan women, Rome. He says that she, urging the other Trojan women, in common with them burned the vessels, being weighed down by the wandering. With him agree also Damastes of Sigeum and certain others. 72.3. But Aristotle the philosopher relates that certain of the Achaeans, of those returning from Troy, sailing round Malea, then caught by a violent storm, were for a time borne by the winds and wandered over many parts of the sea, and at last came to this place of Opica, which is called Latinium, lying upon the Tyrrhenian Sea. 72.4. Glad to see the land, they hauled up their ships there and spent the winter season, preparing to sail at the beginning of spring. But their ships being burned by night, having no means to make their departure, by an unwilling necessity they fixed their lives in the place where they had put in. And this befell them through the captive women whom they chanced to be leading from Ilium. These burned the ships, fearing the departure of the Achaeans homeward, as they would come into slavery. 72.5. But Callias, who recorded the deeds of Agathocles, says that a certain Trojan woman, Rome, of those who came with the other Trojans into Italy, was married to Latinus the king of the Aborigines and bore three sons, Romus and Romulus and Telegonus . . . and that, having founded a city, they gave it its name after their mother. But Xenagoras the historian says that of Odysseus and Circe were born three sons, Romus, Anteias, Ardeias; and that, having founded three cities, they gave their own names to the foundations. 72.6. But Dionysius of Chalcis declares the founder of the city to be Romus; and this man, he says, was according to some the son of Ascanius, according to others of Emathion. And there are some who say that Rome was founded by Romus the son of Italus, his mother being Leucaria the daughter of Latinus. 73.1. Though I am able to produce many others too of the Greek historians, who declare different founders of the city, yet, that I may not seem to be long-winded, I shall come to the Roman historians. Now there is not a single ancient historian or chronicler among the Romans; but each, taking something from ancient accounts preserved in sacred tablets, has set it down. 73.2. Of these, some say that the sons of Aeneas were Romulus and Romus, the founders of Rome; others, that they were the sons of a daughter of Aeneas, no longer defining by what father; and that they were given by Aeneas to Latinus the king of the Aborigines as hostages, at the time when the pledges between the inhabitants and the newcomers were made. And Latinus, welcoming them, treated them well with other attentions, and, dying without male offspring, left them successors to a part of his rule. 73.3. Others say that, Aeneas having died, Ascanius, taking over the whole rule of the Latins, divided with his brothers Romulus and Romus both the land and the power of the Latins in three; that he himself founded Alba and certain other towns; that Romus founded Capua, from his great-grandfather Capys, and Anchisa, from his ancestor Anchises, and Aeneia, afterward called Janiculum, from his father, and Rome, from himself; and that this last, having been desolate for some time, when another colony came—which the Albans sent under the leadership of Romulus and Romus—recovered its ancient foundation; so that there were two foundings of Rome, the one occurring a little after the Trojan times, the other fifteen generations later than the former. 73.4. And if one wishes to look at things still further back, a third Rome, more ancient than these, will be found to have existed before Aeneas and the Trojans came to Italy. This no chance writer nor recent historian has recorded, but Antiochus of Syracuse, whom I mentioned before. He says that, while Morges reigned in Italy (and Italy was then the coast from Tarentum to Posidonia), there came to him a man, an exile from Rome, named Sicelus. He speaks thus: "And when Italus grew old, Morges reigned. In his time there came a man, an exile from Rome; Sicelus was his name." 73.5. According to the Syracusan historian, then, a certain ancient Rome is found, prior even to the Trojan times. But whether it was about the same places in which the now inhabited city stands, or some other place chanced to be so named, I am unable to conjecture, since he left that unclear. Concerning the ancient foundings, then, I think what has been said before sufficient. 74.1. As for the last settlement, or founding, of Rome—or whatever one ought to call it—Timaeus of Sicily, by what canon I know not, says it took place at the same time as the founding of Carthage, in the thirty-eighth year before the first Olympiad. But Lucius Cincius, a man of the senatorial order, places it about the fourth year of the twelfth Olympiad; and Quintus Fabius in the first year of the eighth Olympiad. 74.2. Porcius Cato does not define the time in the Greek manner, but, being careful as any other in the gathering of antiquarian history, declares it to be four hundred and thirty-two years later than the Trojan events. This time, measured against the chronicles of Eratosthenes, falls in the first year of the seventh Olympiad. That the canons which Eratosthenes used are sound, and how one might adjust the Roman times to the Greek, has been shown by me in another work. 74.3. For I did not think it right, like Polybius of Megalopolis, to say only so much, that I am persuaded Rome was founded in the second year of the seventh Olympiad, nor to leave the proof untested upon the single tablet kept with the high priests, but to set forth in public the reckonings to which I myself have adhered, that they may be open to scrutiny by any who wish. 74.4. The exact account, then, is made plain in that work, but the most necessary points shall be told through this treatise also. It is thus. The incursion of the Celts, in which the city of Rome was taken, is agreed by almost all to have occurred when Pyrgion was archon at Athens, in the first year of the ninety-eighth Olympiad. And the time before the capture, carried back to Lucius Junius Brutus and Lucius Tarquinius Collatinus, the first to be consuls at Rome after the abolition of the kings, comprises a hundred and twenty years. 74.5. This is made plain from many other things and from the so-called censorial records, which a son receives from his father and sets great store by handing on to those who shall come after him, like ancestral sacred objects; and there are many distinguished men from the censorial houses who preserve them. Among these I find that, in the second year before the capture, a census of the Roman people took place, to which is appended, as to the others, this date: "In the consulship of Lucius Valerius Potitus and Titus Mallius Capitolinus, in the hundred and nineteenth year after the expulsion of the kings." 74.6. So that the Celtic incursion, which we find occurred in the second year after the census, came to pass when the hundred and twenty years had been completed. And if this interval of time is found to be that of thirty Olympiads, it must be admitted that the first consuls appointed took over their office when Isagoras was archon at Athens, in the first year of the sixty-eighth Olympiad. 75.1. Moreover, the time carried up from the expulsion of the kings to Romulus, the first to rule the city, makes two hundred and forty-four years. This is recognized by the successions of the kings and the years in which each held the rule. For Romulus, who founded the city, is said to have held power thirty-seven years; and after the death of Romulus the city was without a king for the space of a year. 75.2. Then Numa Pompilius, chosen by the people, reigned three-and-forty years; and Tullus Hostilius after Numa two-and-thirty; and he who reigned after him, Ancus Marcius, four-and-twenty; and after Marcius, Lucius Tarquinius, called Priscus, eight-and-thirty; and succeeding him, Servius Tullius, four-and-forty; and he who slew Servius, Lucius Tarquinius, the tyrannical and, for his contempt of justice, called Superbus, carried his rule on to a twenty-fifth year. 75.3. The two hundred and forty-four years which the kings held being filled out, and sixty-one Olympiads, it is altogether necessary that the first ruler of the city, Romulus, took over the kingdom in the first year of the seventh Olympiad, when Charops was archon at Athens, in the first year of his ten-year term. For so the reckoning of the years requires. And that each of the kings ruled so many years is made plain by me through that other work. 75.4. Such, then, are the things said by those before me concerning the time at which the now ruling city was founded, and as they seem to me. As for who its founders were, and by what fortunes they sent out the colony, and whatever else has been recorded about this founding, many things have been said by many, and most differently by some; but I too shall tell the most probable of the things remembered. It is thus. 76.1. When Amulius took over the kingdom of the Albans, having barred his elder brother Numitor from his ancestral honour by overpowering him, he both did all else with great contempt of justice, and at last plotted to make the house of Numitor bereft of offspring, through fear of paying the penalty and through love of never being deprived of the rule. 76.2.
