Having long planned these things, he first watched for Numitor's son Aegestus, just coming to manhood, where he hunted, and, having laid an ambush in the most secret part of the place, slew him as he went out to the hunt, and contrived that it should be said after the deed that the youth had been killed by robbers. Yet the fabricated opinion did not prevail over the truth that was hushed up, but by many, even at the risk of safety, the deed was ventured to be spoken of. 76.3. Numitor knew of the deed, but, using a calculation stronger than his suffering, feigned ignorance, having resolved to defer his anger to a less dangerous time. Amulius, supposing the matter of the youth to have escaped notice, did this second thing: Numitor's daughter Ilia—or, as some write, Rhea by name, Silvia by surname—being in the bloom of marriageable age, he appointed priestess of Hestia, so that she might not, coming too soon to a husband, bear avengers for the race. For not less than five years the sacred maidens had to remain pure of marriage, to whom was assigned the guarding of the unquenchable fire and whatever else it was customary for the commonwealth to have performed through virgins. 76.4. Amulius did this under fair names, as though investing the race with honour and adornment, neither having himself introduced this law, nor being the first to compel his brother, though of equal rank, to make use of it from among those in dignity, but it being customary among the Albans and held honourable to appoint the noblest maidens attendants of Hestia. And Numitor, perceiving that his brother did these things not from the best motive, made no open show of anger, that he might not be hated by the people, but kept this complaint too secret. 77.1. Four years later, Ilia, having come to a sacred grove of Ares for the fetching of pure water, which she was to use for the sacrifices, was violated by someone in the precinct. This man some declare to have been one of the suitors of the maiden, in love with the girl; others, Amulius himself, not so much for desire as for plotting, having fenced himself with arms so as to appear most terrifying, and rendering the familiar look of his face as obscure as he could. 77.2. But the greater part tell in legend that it was an apparition of the divinity to whom the place belonged, attaching many other divine works to the event—a sudden vanishing of the sun and a darkness that held the sky; and a look, which the apparition too had, far more marvellous than that of men in size and beauty. And they say that the one who did the violence, consoling the maiden's grief, said—whence it became plain that he was a god—that she should be in no way distressed at what had befallen; for the partnership of marriage had come to her with the divinity who haunted the place, and that she would bear from the violence two sons, far the mightiest of men in virtue and in war. And having said this, he was wrapped in a cloud and, raised from the earth, was borne up through the air. 77.3. Now in what manner one ought to hold an opinion concerning such things—whether to despise them as human fabrications referred to the gods, since the god would undertake no service unworthy of the imperishable and blessed nature, or to admit these accounts too, on the supposition that the whole substance of the universe is intermingled, and that between the divine and the mortal race there exists a certain third nature, which the tribe of divinities occupies, mingling now with men, now with gods, from which the account has it that the legendary race of heroes is sprung—it is no time at present to examine; and what has been said by the philosophers about them suffices. 77.4. The maiden, then, after the violence, feigning sickness (for this her mother counselled her, both for safety and for the duties owed to the gods), no longer approached the sacred rites, but the other virgins, to whom the same office was assigned, performed all that she had to minister. 78.1. Amulius, whether moved by consciousness of what had been done or led by suspicion of the likely, made inquiry into the cause of the long absence of the maiden from the sacred rites—sending in physicians whom he most trusted, and, when the women alleged the disease to be one not to be spoken of to men, leaving his own wife as a guard over the maiden. 78.2. And when she became an accuser of the case, having found out by womanly conjecture what was hidden from the others, he set a guard of arms over the girl, lest she should bear unobserved (for she was not far from her time); and he himself, calling his brother to the council, became an informer of the corruption that had escaped the others, and accused the parents of conniving with the girl, and bade them not 78.3. hide the doer, but bring him to light. Numitor said that he was hearing strange words and was guiltless of all that was alleged, and asked to be given time for the testing of the truth; and obtaining the postponement with difficulty, when he had learned the matter from the woman, as the girl had at first related, he set forth both the violence done by the god, and went through the words spoken by him concerning the twin sons, and asked that this be made the proof of what was said, if the offspring of the travail should be such as the god had foretold. For the girl was close upon bearing, so that it would not appear, after long, to be a fabrication. And he delivered up the women guarding the girl and 78.4. shrank from no proof. While he spoke these things, the multitude of the council was persuaded; but Amulius declared nothing sound in what was asked, and from every quarter was bent on destroying the woman. While these things were going on, those appointed to guard the travail came in, declaring that the girl had borne twin male infants; and at once Numitor was again abundant in the same argument, showing the deed to be the god's, and asking that no wrong be done to the girl, who was guiltless of what had befallen; while to Amulius the matter of the birth too seemed to be some human contrivance, another infant having been provided for the women, either secretly from the guards or with their connivance; and 78.5. much was said to this effect. And when the councillors learned the king's purpose, which was using an inexorable anger, they too thought it right, as he asked, to make use of the law, which bade her who had defiled her body be scourged with rods and die, and the offspring be cast into the stream of the river; though now the law concerning the sacred rites prescribes that such women be buried alive. 79.1. Up to this point most of the historians declare the same things, or differing a little, some toward the more legendary, others toward what is more like the truth; but concerning what follows they are at variance. 79.2. For some say that the girl was straightway put to death; others, that she continued to be kept in a secret prison, giving the people the opinion of an unseen death. And that Amulius was bent to this by his daughter, who entreated him to grant her the cousin as a favour; for they were foster-companions and of the same age, and embraced one another as sisters. Gratifying her, then—and she was his only daughter—Amulius released Ilia from death, but kept her shut up in concealment; and she was in time released, Amulius having died. 79.3. Concerning Ilia, then, the writings of the ancients thus differ, and both have reason as being true. For this cause I too have made mention of both, and which one ought to believe each of the readers will himself decide. 79.4. Concerning those born of Ilia, Quintus Fabius, called Pictor—whom Lucius Cincius and Porcius Cato and Calpurnius Piso and most of the other historians followed—has written thus: that, Amulius having commanded it, certain of the servants, taking the infants as they lay in a trough, carried them to cast into the river, which is distant from the city about a hundred and twenty stades. 79.5. But when they came near and saw the Tiber, swollen by continual storms, turned out of its proper bed into the plains, descending from the summit of the Pallantium to the nearest water (for they were no longer able to go farther), where first the flood of the river touched the foothills, they set the trough upon the water. It floated for a time; then, the stream gradually receding, the trough, overturned by striking against a stone at the edges, cast out the infants. 79.6. They, whimpering, were rolled about in the mud; and a she-wolf appeared, lately delivered, her dugs swollen with milk, who gave her teats to their mouths and licked off with her tongue the mud with which they were covered. Meanwhile the herdsmen chanced to be driving their flocks out to pasture (for the place was already passable), and one of them, seeing the wolf as she fondled the infants, was for a time speechless from amazement and disbelief at what he saw; then, going off and gathering as many as he could of those grazing near (for they did not believe him when he told it), he led them to behold the thing itself. 79.7. And when these too, coming near, saw the wolf tending them as her own young, and the infants clinging to her as to a mother, supposing they beheld some divine thing, they came nearer in a body, frightening the beast with shouting. But the she-wolf, not at all made savage by the men's approach, but, as if tamed, withdrawing gently from the infants and with great disregard of the company of shepherds, went off. 79.8. And there was not far from there a sacred place, roofed over with deep wood, and a hollow rock sending up springs; and the glen was said to be Pan's, and there was an altar of the god there. Coming to this place, the wolf hid herself. The grove no longer remains; but the cave, from which the spring issues, is shown built up against the Pallantium, along the road leading to the hippodrome; and there is a precinct of him near, where lies an image of the event, a she-wolf holding out her teats to two children, bronze works of ancient workmanship. The place was sacred, as is said, to the Arcadians who once settled it with Evander. 79.9. When the beast withdrew, the herdsmen took up the infants, eager to rear them, as the gods wished them to be saved. And there was among them one who had charge of the royal swine-herds, a reasonable man, Faustulus by name, who had been in the city on some necessary business at the time when the corruption of Ilia and the birth were being investigated, and afterward, when the infants were being carried to the river, by a divine chance had gone along the same road with those bearing them, on his way to the Pallantium; and he, least of all making it plain to the others that he knew something of the matter, having asked that the infants be granted him, took them from the company and went off with them to his wife. 79.10. Finding her delivered and grieving that her infant was born dead, he consoled her and gave her the children to substitute as her own, having related from the beginning all the fortune that had befallen them. As they grew, he gave the name Romulus to the one, Romus to the other. And these, when grown to manhood, became, in dignity of form and pride of spirit, not like swineherds and cowherds, but such as one would deem those born of a royal race and held to be of divine begetting, as is sung by the Romans even now in their ancestral hymns. 79.11. Their life was that of herdsmen, and their diet self-provided, dwelling for the most part in the mountains, having built themselves huts, self-roofed, of wood and reeds; one of which, even down to my time, was on the side of the Pallantium turning toward the hippodrome, called the hut of Romulus, which those who have charge of these things keep sacred, adding nothing to make it more august, but, if it suffers anything from storm or time, repairing the loss and likening it to its former state as far as possible. 79.12. When they were about eighteen years old, a dispute arose for them concerning the pasture against the herdsmen of Numitor, who had their cattle-stations about the Aventine mountain, lying over against the Pallantium. And each accused the other frequently of either grazing the pasture that did not belong to them, or of holding the common pasture for themselves alone, or whatever it chanced to be. From this skirmishing there came at times blows by hand, then by arms. 79.13. Numitor's men, having received many wounds from the youths and having lost some of their own, and being now forcibly excluded from the lands, prepared some treachery against them. Laying an ambush in the hidden part of the ravine, and having agreed with those lying in wait for the youths upon the moment of attack, the rest in a body fell by night upon their folds. Romulus chanced at this time to have gone, with the most distinguished of the villagers, to a place called Caenina, to perform the ancestral sacred rites on behalf of the commonwealth; 79.14. but Romus, perceiving their attack, sallied out to the rescue with his arms in haste, taking with him a few of those from the village who had contrived to gather as one. And they did not await him, but fled, drawing him on to where they meant, turning back at a fitting moment, to fall upon him; and Romus, in ignorance of the contrivance, pursuing them a long way, passed the place where the ambush lay, and thereupon the ambush rose and the fugitives turned back. Surrounding him and pelting him with many stones, they took him into their hands. For they had this charge from their masters, to bring the young men to them alive. Thus, then, was Romus overcome and led away. 80.1. But as Aelius Tubero, an able man and careful in the gathering of history, writes, Numitor's men, knowing beforehand that the youths would sacrifice the Lupercalia—the Arcadian sacrifice to Pan, as Evander established it—laid an ambush for that moment of the rite, when those of the young men dwelling about the Pallantium had, after sacrificing at the Lupercal, to run round the village naked, girded about their loins with the skins of the newly slain victims. This served as a kind of ancestral purification of the villagers, 80.2. as is still done even now. At this time, then, the cowherds, having lain in wait for the youths who were performing the rites at the narrow part of the road, when the first company, that with Romus, came opposite them—those about Romulus and the others lagging behind (for they were divided in three and ran at intervals)—not waiting for the rest, rushed upon the first, shouting in a body, and surrounding them, pelted them, some with javelins, some with stones, some with whatever each had at hand. And they, astounded by the unexpectedness of the misfortune and at a loss what to do, fighting unarmed against armed men, were with great ease overcome. 80.3. Romus, then, having thus fallen into the enemy's hands, was, as Fabius has handed down, led away bound to Alba. And Romulus, when he learned the misfortune of his brother, thought he ought at once to pursue, with the most vigorous of the herdsmen, so as to overtake Romus while still upon the road; but he was turned aside by Faustulus. For seeing his eagerness to be too frenzied, this man, who was thought to be his father, the things which in the former time he had kept secret from the youths—lest they should too soon set out to venture something before they were at the height of their prime—then, being constrained by necessity, told to Romulus when he was alone. 80.4. And when the young man had learned from the beginning all the fortune that had befallen them, pity for his mother came upon him and care for Numitor; and after much deliberation with Faustulus, it seemed best to restrain his immediate impulse, and, using a greater preparation of force, to free the whole house from the lawlessness of Amulius and to hazard the utmost danger for the greatest prizes, and to act with his maternal grandfather in whatever should seem good to him. 81.1. When this seemed best, Romulus, calling together all the villagers and bidding them hasten to Alba speedily—not all entering by the same gates nor in a body, lest some suspicion arise toward those in the city, but waiting about the marketplace, ready to do what was commanded— 81.2. went off first to the city. And those leading Romus, when they had set him before the king, accused him of all the insolences with which they had been outraged by the youths, and showed their wounded, foretelling that, if they should not obtain redress, they would abandon the cattle-herds. And Amulius, wishing to gratify the countrymen who had come in a body, and Numitor (for he chanced to be present, sharing the indignation of his retainers), and eager that there should be peace throughout the country, and at the same time taking in suspicion the boldness of the youth, as he was undismayed in his words, gave judgment against him; and he made Numitor master of the punishment, saying that to one who has done dread things the requital is owed by none other more than the one who has suffered. 81.3. While Romus was being led by Numitor's cowherds, his hands bound behind, and mocked by those leading him, Numitor, following, marvelled at the comeliness of his body, how much of the royal it had, and pondered the nobility of his spirit, which he preserved even amid the terrors, turning neither to lamentation nor to entreaties, as all do in such fortunes, but going to his death with seemly silence. 81.4. When they came to the house, bidding the others withdraw, he asked Romus, now alone, who he was and of what parents, since such a man could not have been born of common folk. And when Romus said that he knew only this much, from the inquiry of his foster-father, that he had been exposed an infant in a glen with a twin brother straightway from birth, and, taken up by the herdsmen, had been reared, Numitor, having waited a short time—whether suspecting something of the truth or led by the divinity to bring the matter to light—said to him: 81.5. "That you are in my power, Romus, to suffer whatever I shall judge, and that those who brought you here, having suffered many dread things, would set great store by your death, there is no need to say to one who knows it. But if I should release you from death and from every other evil, would you know gratitude to me, and, at my asking, render a service that shall be a common good to us both?" 81.6. When the youth answered all that the hope of being saved prompts those lying in despair of life to say and promise to those who have power over it, Numitor, bidding him be loosed and all withdraw out of the way, told him his own fortunes: how Amulius, being his brother, had deprived him of the kingdom and made him bereft of children—the one having been secretly made away with at the hunt, the other kept bound in prison—and all else with which a master, using a slave, does outrage. 82.1. Having said this, and pouring out much lamentation along with his words, he asked Romus to become the avenger of the evils of his house. And when the youth gladly received the proposal and asked to be set to the deed at once, Numitor, praising his zeal, said: "I shall husband the moment for the action; but you, meanwhile, send to your brother a message secret to all others, declaring that you are safe, and asking him to come speedily." 82.2. Thereupon one was found and sent who seemed likely to be of service; and falling in with Romulus, who was not far from the city, he made plain the message. He, overjoyed, came in haste to Numitor, and embracing both, greeted them first, then told of their exposure and rearing and all else that he had learned from Faustulus. And to those who wished it, and who needed no many proofs to believe, what was said was pleasing. When they had recognized one another, at once they laid plans together and considered what would be the 82.3. manner or fitting moment for the attack. While these were thus engaged, Faustulus was led off to Amulius. For, fearing that Romulus might not seem to Numitor to speak credibly, having become the informer of a great matter without manifest signs, he had taken up the trough, the token of the infants' exposure, and a little later followed into the city. 82.4. As he passed the gates in great agitation, taking much care to make plain to no one what he carried, one of the guards observed him (for there was fear of an enemy's incursion, and the gates were guarded by those most trusted by the king), and seizing him and demanding to learn the hidden thing, whatever it was, he uncovered the cloak by force. And when he saw the trough and perceived that the man was at a loss, he asked him to say what the agitation was, and what the purpose of not openly carrying a vessel that needed no secret bearing. 82.5. Meanwhile more of the guards ran together, and one of them recognized the trough, having himself carried the children in it to the river, and told those present. And they, seizing Faustulus, led him to the king himself and related what had happened. 82.6. Amulius, having terrified the man with the threat of tortures if he should not willingly speak the truth, first asked whether the children were alive; and when he learned this, what was the manner of their preservation; and when he had related all as it was done, the king said: "Come now, since you have spoken these things truly, tell me where they may now be found. For they are no longer rightly to live among herdsmen and an inglorious life, being kinsmen of mine, especially as they are preserved by the providence of the gods." 83.1. Faustulus, moved by suspicion at the unreasonable mildness, that the king's thoughts were not like his words, answered thus: "The children are in the mountains tending cattle, which is their life; and I was sent by them to their mother to make plain in what fortunes they are; and hearing that she is kept in your custody, I was about to ask your daughter to lead me to her. The trough I carried that I might be able to show a manifest proof along with my words. Now, then, since you have resolved to bring the young men hither, I rejoice, and do you send whom you wish with me. I shall show the children to those who come, and they shall tell them your message." 83.2. He said this, wishing to find a postponement of death for the children, and at the same time hoping himself to escape those leading him when he came into the mountains. But Amulius, secretly charging the most trusted of his armed men to seize whomever the swineherd should point out and bring them to him, sent them off in haste. Having done this, he at once formed the resolve to call his brother and hold him in unbound custody until he should set the present matters well, and he summoned him as though for some 83.3. other purpose. But the messenger sent, yielding to goodwill toward the one in danger and pity for his fortune, became an informer to Numitor of Amulius's purpose. And he, having made plain to the youths the danger that had befallen them and exhorting them to be brave men, came leading armed men to the palace—of his other retainers and companions and faithful attendants no small band. There came too those who had gathered from the fields into the city, having abandoned the marketplace, holding swords hidden beneath their cloaks, a strong body. And forcing the entrance, all with one onset, guarded as it was by no many men-at-arms, they easily slew Amulius and after this seized the citadel. These things, then, are stated by those about Fabius. 84.1. But others, thinking that nothing too legendary befits historical writing, say that the exposure of the infants, not made as the servants were ordered, is incredible, and they deride as full of dramatic absurdity the tameness of the she-wolf that held out her teats to the children. 84.2. And, exchanging these for other accounts, they say that Numitor, when he learned that Ilia was pregnant, having provided other newborn children, substituted them when she had borne her infants, and gave the strangers' children to those guarding the travail to carry off—whether having bought the trust of their service with money or having contrived the substitution through women—and Amulius, taking them, made away with them in some manner; while the offspring of Ilia, the maternal grandfather, esteeming it of the utmost moment that they be saved, gave to Faustulus. 84.3. This Faustulus they say was an Arcadian by race, of those with Evander, and dwelt about the Pallantium, having charge of Amulius's possessions; and that he gratified Numitor in the rearing of the children, being persuaded by his brother, named Faustinus, who had charge of Numitor's herds, reared about the Aventine. 84.4. And the one who nursed the children and held out her teats they say was no she-wolf, but, as is likely, a woman dwelling with Faustulus, named Laurentia, on whom—once making public the bloom of her body—those tarrying about the Pallantium had laid the surname Lupa (she-wolf). This is a Greek and ancient term applied to those who hire out their bodies for love, who are now called by the more seemly name hetaerae. And certain men, in ignorance of this, fabricated the legend of the she-wolf, since in the tongue which the Latin people speak this animal is called lupa. When the children were weaned from the milk-diet, they were given by those rearing them to the city of Gabii, lying not far from the 84.5. Pallantium, that they might learn Greek education; and there, with men who were private guest-friends of Faustulus, they were reared, being taught letters and music and the use of Greek arms until manhood. 84.6. And when they came to their reputed parents, the dispute befell them against Numitor's cowherds concerning the common pasture-lands; and from this, having given them blows, they drove off the herds to themselves; and they did this by the design of Numitor, that there might be a beginning of complaints and at the same time a pretext for the coming of the herdsman 84.7. multitude into the city. When this had happened, Numitor cried out against Amulius, that he was suffering dreadful things, being plundered by that man's cowherds, and demanded, if he were the cause of nothing, that he deliver up to him the cattle-keeper and his sons for trial; and Amulius, wishing to clear himself of the charge, bade both those asked for and all the others who had the charge of being present at what was done to come and submit to trial before Numitor. 84.8. And when many had gathered together with the accused under the pretext of the trial, the maternal grandfather, having made plain to the young men all the fortune that had befallen them and having said that now was the moment, if ever, to take vengeance, at once with the herdsman multitude made the attack. Concerning the birth and rearing of the founders of Rome, then, these things are said. 85.1. The events concerning the founding itself (for this part of my writing still remains to me) I now come to relate. When, Amulius having died, Numitor renewed his rule, after waiting a short time, in which he ordered the city from its former disorder into the ancient fashion, he straightway purposed to provide a rule of their own for the youths by settling another city. 85.2. At the same time, the citizen multitude having increased in numbers, he thought it well to expend some of it, and especially that which had once been at variance with him, that he might not hold them in suspicion. Having communicated with the youths, when it seemed good to them too, he gave them lands over which they should rule, where as children they had been reared, and from the people both the one who had been a cause of suspicion to him, who was likely to begin some revolution hereafter, and any who wished to remove of their own will. 85.3. Among these was much, as is natural in a city in commotion, of the common sort; sufficient also of the notable from the best class; and, of the Trojan element, what was reckoned the most noble, of which some families still survived in my time, about fifty houses. And the young men were supplied with money and arms and corn and slaves and beasts of burden and whatever else was useful for the equipment of a city. 85.4. When the young men had set out from Alba, mingling with their people that from the place itself, as much as was left in the Pallantium and about the Saturnia, they divided the whole multitude in two. This gave them an opinion of emulation, that the works might be accomplished more quickly through their rivalry with one another, but became the cause of the greatest evil, dissension. 85.5. For those allotted to each, each magnifying their own leader as fit to rule over all, exalted him; and they themselves, no longer holding one mind nor thinking it right to deliberate as brothers, each as one who would himself rule the other, thrusting aside equality, reached out for the greater. For a time, then, their graspings were unseen; but afterward they broke out on this pretext. 85.6. The place where they were to set up the city each chose not the same. For it was Romulus's opinion to settle the Pallantium, both for other reasons and for the fortune of the place, which had granted them to be saved and reared; but to Romus it seemed best to settle what is now called from him Remoria. The place fit to receive a city is a hill lying not far from the Tiber, distant from Rome about thirty stades. From this contention straightway an uncommunicating love of rule was hinted; for to the one who yielded the prevailing one was likely to set himself in all things alike. 86.1. Some time having elapsed in this, when the dissension in no way diminished, both resolving to leave it to their maternal grandfather, they came to Alba. And he suggested to them this: to make the gods judges, of which of them the colony ought to be said to belong and the leadership to be. Appointing them a day, he bade them sit from dawn, apart from one another, in such seats as each thought fit; and, having first sacrificed to the gods the customary rites, to watch for auspicious omens; and to whichever the birds should first appear favourable, 86.2. that one should rule the colony. The young men departed, approving this, and according to the agreement came on the appointed day of the action. Romulus's place of augury, where he thought fit to found the colony, was the Pallantium, and Romus's the hill adjoining it, called the Aventine, or, as some relate, the Remoria; and a guard was present for both, not to permit them to say anything but what should appear. 86.3. When they had taken their proper seats, after a short time Romulus, through eagerness and envy toward his brother—and perhaps the god too thus prompted him—before he had even seen any sign whatever, sending messengers to his brother, asked him to come speedily, as having first seen auspicious omens. While those sent by him, holding the deception in shame, went without haste, six vultures appeared to Romus, flying from the right. And he, seeing the birds, was overjoyed; but a little later those sent by Romulus, raising him up, led him to the Pallantium. 86.4. When they were in the same place, Romus asked Romulus what omens he had seen first; and he was at a loss what to answer. Meanwhile twelve auspicious vultures were seen flying, and, seeing them, he took heart, and showing them to Romus, said: "Why do you think it right to learn of what happened long ago? For these omens, surely, you see yourself." But he was indignant and made a great matter of it, as having been deceived by him, and said he would not yield him the colony. 87.1. From this there arose a strife greater than the former, each secretly claiming to have the more, but openly attaching the claim of not having the less, from such a justification as this. For it had been said to them by their maternal grandfather, that whoever should first have favourable birds appear to him should rule the colony; and one kind of birds having appeared to both, the one was strengthened by having seen them first, the other by having seen the more. And the rest of the multitude joined in their contention, and began a war, armed without their leaders; and there was a strong battle and much slaughter on both sides. 87.2. In this battle some say that Faustulus, who had reared the young men, wishing to dissolve the strife of the brothers, when he was able to accomplish nothing, thrust himself unarmed among the combatants, eager to meet the swiftest death—which indeed came to pass. Some say also that the stone lion which lay in the marketplace of the Romans, in the strongest place beside the rostra, was set over the body of Faustulus, who was buried there where he fell by those who found him. 87.3. Romus having died in the battle, Romulus, having won a most pitiable victory over his brother and from civil mutual slaughter, buried Romus in the Remoria, since even in life he had clung to that place for the founding, while he himself, through grief and repentance for what had been done, abandoning himself, turned to despair of life. But, Laurentia—who, taking them as newborns, had reared them and embraced them no less than a mother—entreating and consoling him, persuaded by her he rose up; and gathering the Latins, as many as had not been destroyed in the battle, being a little more than three thousand out of a very great multitude at the beginning, when he sent out the colony, 87.4. he built the Pallantium into a city. This, then, seems to me the most credible of the accounts concerning the death of Romus. But let it nonetheless be told if any other version has been handed down. Some say that he yielded the leadership to Romulus, but, vexed and holding the deception in anger, when the wall had been built, wishing to show the bulwark feeble, said: "But this at least an enemy might easily leap over, as I do"—and at once leapt over it; and that a certain Celer, one of those who had mounted the wall, who was overseer of the works, saying, "But this enemy at least one of us might easily ward off," struck him with his spade upon the head and at once killed him. Such, then, is said to have been the end of the dissension of the brothers. 88.1. When there was no longer anything in the way of the foundation, Romulus, having proclaimed a day on which, after propitiating the gods, he meant to make the beginning of the works, and having prepared whatever was to be of use for sacrifices and the reception of the people, when the appointed time came, himself having first sacrificed to the gods and bidden the others do the same as far as they were able, first took auspicious birds; and after this, having bidden bonfires be made before the tents, he led the people out to leap over the flames, for the hallowing away of pollutions. When all that was by reckoning 88.2. dear to the gods seemed to him to have been done, calling all to the appointed place, he traced a four-square figure about the hill, drawing, with a male ox yoked together with a female under the plough, a continuous furrow that was to receive the wall; from which this custom of ploughing round the bounds in the founding of cities remains among the Romans. Having done this and sacrificed each of the oxen, and begun the rites of many other victims, he set the people to the works. This day even 88.3. down to my time the city of the Romans keeps every year, accounting it inferior to no festival, and they call it the Parilia. On it the husbandmen and herdsmen sacrifice a thank-offering concerning the breeding of four-footed creatures at the beginning of spring. But whether, still earlier, passing this day in festivities, they deemed it most fitting for the founding of a city, or, since it began the foundation, they made it sacred and thought right to honour on it the gods dear to shepherds, I cannot say with certainty. 89.1. What, then, I have been able with much care to find out, having read through many writings of Greeks and Romans concerning the race of the Romans, is this. So that anyone may now confidently declare, bidding a long farewell to those who make Rome a refuge of barbarians and runaways and homeless men, that it is a Greek city—showing it to be the most communal of cities and the most humane, reflecting that the tribe of the Aborigines was Oenotrian, and this Arcadian; 89.2. and calling to mind the Pelasgians who settled with them, who, leaving Thessaly, being Argives by race, came to Italy; and again the coming of Evander and the Arcadians, who dwelt about the Pallantium, the Aborigines having furnished them the place; and besides, the Peloponnesians who came with Heracles, who settled upon the Saturnius; and last, those who set out from the Troad and were blended with the former. For of these peoples one would find none either more ancient or more Greek. 89.3. But the minglings with the barbarians, through which the city unlearned many of its ancient pursuits, came about in time. And this might seem a marvel to many who reckon the probabilities—how the whole was not made barbarous, when it received Opicans and Marsians and Samnites and Tyrrhenians and Bruttians, and many myriads of Umbrians and Ligurians and Iberians and Celts, and besides those mentioned, peoples beyond number, some come from Italy itself, others from other places, of neither like tongue nor like manner of life, whose mingled and confused ways of life, disordered by so great a discord, were likely to have made new much of the ancient 89.4. order of the city; since many others, dwelling among barbarians, in a short time unlearned all their Greek character, so as neither to speak the Greek tongue, nor use the pursuits of the Greeks, nor hold the same gods, nor have the equitable laws—by which most of all Greek nature differs from barbarian—nor anything else of their other usages. The Achaeans dwelling about the Pontus suffice to prove this account: being of the Eleans, the most Greek of stocks, they are now the most savage of all barbarians. 90.1. But the Romans speak a tongue neither utterly barbarous nor perfectly Greek, but a certain mixture of both, of which the greater part is Aeolic—having reaped this alone from their many minglings, that they do not speak correctly in all their sounds; but all else, as many tokens as there are of a Greek race, they preserve as no others of those who have founded colonies, not now for the first time beginning to live in friendship, when they have fortune flowing rich and good as a teacher of noble things, nor from the time when they first reached out for dominion overseas, having overthrown the rule of the Carthaginians and Macedonians, but from all the time since they were settled together, living a Greek life and pursuing nothing more distinguished toward virtue now than before. 90.2. Though I have countless things to say to this end, and am able to use many proofs and to bring forward the testimonies of men not worthy to be disbelieved, I defer all these to the work to be written concerning their constitution. But now I shall turn to the narrative that follows, having made the recapitulation of what has been set forth in this book the beginning of the writing that comes next.

The city of Rome lies in the western part of Italy upon the river Tiber, which empties into the sea at about the middle of the coast, and it is distant a hundred and twenty stades from the Tyrrhenian Sea. For whenever he saw fit to lead out an army, there was then no need to appoint tribunes by tribes, or centurions by companies, or commanders of horse, or for each to be numbered off, formed into companies, and assigned his proper post; but the king gave the word to the tribunes, they to the captains, and from these the decurions, receiving it, led out each the men under his own command; and at a single word of command, whether the whole force or some portion of it was summoned, it was present, armed and ready, at the appointed place.

And he said they were introducing the beginnings of wicked measures, gathering secret councils in private houses, and not even calling all the senators to these, but those most suited to themselves. Now of the other senators excluded from the household council he said he marvelled less; but at the disdain of inviting Marcus Horatius and Lucius Valerius — those who had abolished the oligarchy, consular men and second to none in fitness to deliberate the common affairs — into the council he was astonished, and could not conjecture by what just reasoning; but he guessed at one cause: that, being about to introduce wicked and inexpedient opinions against the commons, they did not wish to summon to these councils the most pro-popular men, who would obviously be indignant and would not overlook any unjust measure being framed against the people.

Yet the people did not take the choice upon itself, but gave the decision to the senators, as being content with whichever of the constitutions they should approve. To them it seemed good, all of them, to establish a kingly constitution; but concerning him who should reign, strife fell out, from which order he should be. For some thought that the one to govern the city ought to be appointed from the ancient senators, others from those brought in later, whom they called the "younger."

When all was ready for battle on both sides, they went out into the plain, and joining battle, fought till midday, neither yielding to the enemy nor gaining, each side ever equalizing the hard-pressed part with those posted in reserve. Herein especially the Aequians and Volscians, exceeding the Romans in number, held up and prevailed, the enemy not having a number equal to their zeal.

Those who formed the conspiracy, then, were destroyed in this manner. And the senate, having voted that all the citizens be purified, because they had been compelled to declare opinions about a civil bloodshed — as not lawful for them to be present at sacred rites and to begin sacrifices before they had expiated the pollution and dissolved the calamity by the customary purifications — when all that was holy had been done by those who interpret divine matters according to the local custom, voted that thank-offerings and games be performed after this, and set apart three days as sacred for these. And Manius Tullius, one of the consuls, having fallen from the sacred chariot in the holy games named after the city, in the procession, in the very hippodrome, and having died on the third day after this procession, Sulpicius alone held the office for the remaining time, which was brief.

Quintius, seeing many of his own dead and most of the survivors wounded, was minded to recall his force; but fearing he might give the enemy the impression of flight, he resolved that they must hazard all. Choosing the best of the horse, on the right, which was most hard pressed, he came to the aid of his men.

These ten men, having drawn up laws from both the Greek laws and the unwritten customs among themselves, set them forth on ten tablets for whoever wished to examine, accepting every correction of private persons and directing what was written toward common satisfaction. And for a long time they continued sitting in council with the best men and making the most exact scrutiny of the legislation.

And partly reproaching the officers themselves for their cowardice, partly reminding them of former contests, partly recounting the disgrace and the danger that would overtake them in flight, at last he said a thing not true, which most of all put courage in his own men and fear in the enemy. For he said that the other of their wings had already driven back the enemy and was now near their camp.

When what was written seemed to them to be sufficient, first, convening the senate, none any longer finding fault with the laws, they ratified a preliminary decree concerning them. Then, calling the people to the centuriate assembly, the keepers of the sacred records and the augurs and the other priests being present and interpreting the divine matters as is the custom, they gave out the votes to the centuries.

So saying, he charged the enemy, and dismounting from his horse, with the picked horsemen about him fought hand to hand. Thereupon a certain daring fell on those till then hard pressed, and all pushed forward as though they had become other men; and the Volscians—for they were drawn up there—after holding out a long time, gave way. When Quintius had driven these back, mounting his horse he rode along to the other line, and pointed out to the foot there the beaten part of the enemy, and exhorted them not to fall short of the others in valour.

The people too having ratified the laws, engraving them on bronze pillars, they set them up in order in the forum, choosing the most conspicuous place. And since the time of their office remaining was short, gathering the senators, they set before them to consider what should be done about the elections.

The contention being drawn out at length, they agreed at last upon this just arrangement: that one of two things should be done — either the elder senators should appoint a king, none of themselves, but whomever of the others they should think most fit; or the younger should do this same thing. The elder accept the choice, and, having taken much counsel among themselves, resolved thus: since they themselves were excluded from the rule by the agreement, to confer the office on none even of the senators who had come in later, but to seek out and appoint as king some man brought in from outside, who would attach himself to neither party, that faction might be most of all removed.

The Veientines, then, having been greatly harmed by that battle, no longer came forth from the city, but endured to see their country sheared. King Tarquinius, having made three invasions and for three years deprived the Veientines of the fruits of their own land, when he had made the most of it desolate and could no longer harm it, led his force against the city of the Caeretani, which formerly was called Agylla while Pelasgians inhabited it, but, having come under the Tyrrhenians, was renamed Caere, and was prosperous, if any other of the cities in Tyrrhenia, and populous;

While these things were being done, there being a tumult in the city as over so great an evil, Tarquinius, learning what was happening through letters, came up leading his force, and about the middle of the night, having got near the city, when the gates were opened by those prepared for the purpose, entered and without effort became master of the city.

The consuls appointed for the coming year were Publius Veturius Geminus and Publius Aebutius Elva. And he declared that the demand of the commoners would no longer be the same as before, nor did he conjecture that the people would come to terms asking only release from debts, but would perhaps need some safeguard by which it might continue secure for the future;

Marcius thought fit to oppose neither of these things, but disputed about their order, thinking he ought to render account first of what had been done by him in the war, then, if it should seem good to all the Volscians, to lay down the command. And of these he thought not one city ought to be master, in which the greater part had been corrupted by Tullus, but the whole nation, gathered into the lawful assembly, to which it was their custom, when they were about to deliberate about the greatest matters, to send delegates from every city.

After this none of the enemy held their ground any longer, but all fled together to the camp. The pursuit of them, however, was not long, but the Romans at once turned back, their bodies slack with toil and their arms no longer in like condition. After a few days had passed, which they had spent in truce for the burial of their own dead and the tending of the worn-out, having repaired what was lacking for the war, they fought another battle around the Roman camp.

Many things being said, the opinion of those advising to appoint a decemvirate again as sovereign of affairs prevailed. For the legislation seemed incomplete, as composed in a short time; and for what was already ratified, that men might willingly and unwillingly abide by it, some sovereign office seemed needed. And what most persuaded them to choose the decemvirate was the dissolution of the tribunes, which they wished most of all.

For he neither killed any of the Gabini nor expelled them from the city nor punished them with loss of citizen rights or confiscation of goods; but, summoning the multitude into an assembly and changing from a tyrannical to a kingly manner, he said he gave them back their own city and conceded to them the property they had, and along with these granted to all the equal citizenship of the Romans — not through goodwill toward the Gabini, but that, by doing this, he might hold the rule of the Romans more securely; thinking the strongest guard of himself and his children would be the faith of those who beyond hope had been saved and had recovered all their own.

But there was no great slaughter of them, the withdrawal into the city not being far off, and those on the walls beating back the pursuers. At these things, suffering naturally, the many were dispirited and had wretched hopes for their safety, since neither consul nor dictator who wished to care for them had been able to, but one of them had even reaped insult and dishonour for his zeal and forethought on behalf of the many. And these things, he said, had been wrought by a conspiracy not of the most gracious of the patricians, but of certain insolent and grasping men, terribly eager for unjust gain, who, having enslaved many citizens for a great difference and at high interest, and applying to them cruel and arrogant compulsions, made the whole commons estranged from the aristocracy; and having formed a faction and proclaimed as its leader Appius Claudius, a man hating the people and oligarchic, through him confound all the city's affairs. And unless the sound part of the senate stood in their way, the city was in danger of some enslavement and overthrow. At the end he declared that he agreed to use the opinion of Menenius, and thought fit to send the embassy quickly; and that the men, when they came, should try to settle the strife as they wished, but, if no one should grant them what they wanted, should accept what was given.

The preliminary decree about the trial is written after this, and a time for the preparation of the defence is fixed for the man up to the third market-day. The market-days came about for the Romans, as even to our times, every ninth day. On these, the commoners coming together from the fields into the city made the exchanges of their wares and took justice from one another, and, taking up the vote, ratified the public matters of which they were master by the laws and which the senate permitted them; but the seven days between the market-days, being for the most part themselves labourers and poor, they spent in the fields.

And for a long while there was much contest, speeches and counter-conflicts going on against one another each day in the assemblies and in the marketplace; for in deed it was not possible for either to force the other, each being secured by the dignity of an equal office.

Quintius, when he learned the multitude of the enemy, received it gladly, and waiting until day came and the hour of full market, perceiving the enemy now worn out by sleeplessness and skirmishes, and not advancing in companies or in order but poured out in many places and scattered, opened the gates of the camp and ran out with the picked horsemen; and the foot, closing up their companies, followed.

There, indeed, the leader of the then decemvirate, Appius, was greatly praised by all, and all the plebeian throng thought fit to keep him in office, as none other would lead better. He pretended at first to refuse and asked to be released from a burdensome and invidious service. But at last, as all entreated him, he both undertook to seek the office, and, charging that the best of those seeking it with him were ill-disposed toward him through envy, openly contended for his own friends.
Having said this, and having sworn by the gods that he spoke the truth, he said that those of the senators who had been called in would clear themselves of all calumny not by words

The city was taken by storm, and the garrison, bound together with the other Tyrrhenian prisoners, was under guard; and of the Fidenates those who seemed to have been responsible for the revolt, some, scourged with whips in public, had their necks cut off, others were penalized with perpetual exile; and their properties the Romans left behind as colonists and as garrison of the city divided by lot.

And, that no fear about the future might remain to them, nor any doubt whether these things would remain firm for them, having written down on what just terms they should be friends, he completed the oaths concerning these matters in the assembly forthwith and swore over the victims. Of these oaths there is a memorial lying at Rome in the temple of Jupiter Pistius, whom the Romans call Sancus — a wooden shield covered with the hide of the ox sacrificed over the oaths at that time, inscribed in archaic letters with the agreements made by them. Having done these things and appointed his son Sextus king of the Gabini, he led off his force. The war against the Gabini, then, had such an end.

About the same time Sextus Tarquinius, leading an army of Latins, campaigned against Signia, which was held by the Romans, as one about to take the fort by assault. The men within fighting back nobly, he had prepared, as one about to compel the people by famine to leave the place, and spent much time there accomplishing nothing worthy of note; but failing of this hope too, supplies and aid coming to the garrison from the consuls, raising the siege he led off his forces.

When the tribunes had received the preliminary decree, going forward into the marketplace they summoned the people to an assembly, and, going through many encomiums of the senate and reading its decrees, proclaimed a day on which they were to complete the trial, to which they thought fit that all the citizens come as men who would decide about the greatest matters.

When no end of the rivalry came about, Tullus, proclaiming a day on which he ordered Marcius to come and lay down his command and undergo trial for treason, and having stirred up the boldest men by hope of benefits to be the authors of an impious deed, came to the appointed assembly and, going up to the tribunal, used much accusation of Marcius, and exhorted the people, if he should not be willing to lay down his command of his own accord, to stop him with all their power.

The Volscians, terrified at their boldness and the frenzied onset, holding out a short time, were thrust back and at the same time gave way from the camp; and—for there was a tolerably high hill not far from the camp—up this they ran, to rest and form again into order. But it was not granted them to form and recover themselves, for the enemy followed hard upon them, closing up their companies as much as possible, that they might not be dashed back forcing their way against high ground.

And he is designated again in the centuriate elections legislator for the second time; and with him Quintus Fabius surnamed Vibulanus, who had been thrice consul, a man up to this time blameless in every virtue; and of the other patricians whom that man favoured, Marcus Cornelius and Marcus Sergius and Lucius Minucius and Titus Antonius and Manius Rabuleius, men not very distinguished; and of the plebeians Quintus Poetelius and Caeso Duellius and Spurius Oppius; for these too were taken in by Appius for the sake of flattering the plebeians, teaching that it was just, when one office was designated over all, that there be some part of the people too in it.

fleeing to the camp, most of them died. For the Romans did not let them go in pursuit, but followed hard on foot, and did not turn back before they had taken their camp by storm. Becoming masters of persons and of all that was left in the camp—horses and arms and very much money—they encamped there that night; on the following day the consul, having prepared what was needful for a siege, led his force against the city of the Antiates, no more than thirty stades distant.

There happened to be present, for the sake of guarding, certain Aequian auxiliaries of the Antiates, watching the walls; who then, fearing the boldness of the Romans, attempted to make their escape from the city. When the Antiates learned of it, being prevented by them from departing, they resolved to hand over the city to the Romans as they approached.

The Antiates, learning this from an informer, yielded to the occasion, and after deliberating in common with those men, handed over the city to Quintius on these terms: that the Aequians depart under truce, and the Antiates receive a garrison and do what the Romans commanded. On these terms the consul became master of the city, and having taken pay and all else the army needed, and established a garrison, he led his force away; in return for which the senate received him with a kindly meeting and honoured him with the procession of a triumph.

Thus far I have nothing to say against those who have given out the history concerning this man; but in what follows I am at a loss what to say. For many are they who have written that Numa was a disciple of Pythagoras, and that at the time he was appointed king by the city of the Romans he was living at Croton studying philosophy; but the time of Pythagoras' age conflicts with the account.

The last battle of the Romans and Tyrrhenians took place near the city of Eretum in the Sabine land. For through that country the Tyrrhenians made their march against the Romans, persuaded by the powerful men there that the Sabines would join the campaign with them. For the six-year truce concerning the peace with Tarquinius had now passed, and many of the Sabines longed to repair their former defeats, a sufficient youth having grown up in the cities.

After this deed Tarquinius, giving the people rest from campaigns and wars, busied himself about the building of the temples, being eager to fulfil the vows of his grandfather. For that man, fighting in his last war against the Sabines, had vowed to Jupiter and Juno and Athena that, if he should prevail in the battle, he would build them temples; and the crag where the gods were to be established he had worked out with great substructures and mounds, as I said in the preceding Book, but had not lived to complete the building of the temples. This work, then, Tarquinius, choosing to accomplish from the tithe of the spoils from Suessa, set all the craftsmen at the labours.

In the following year the Romans appoint as consuls Titus Larcius Flavus and Quintus Cloelius Siculus. Of these, Cloelius was set to manage the city affairs, having the half of the army for the guarding of the revolutionaries, being thought equitable in nature and democratic; but Larcius, leading an army equipped for the war against the Fidenates and having prepared the things fit for a siege, set off.

And not only from the contest-like and earnest dance of the choruses, which the Romans used at the sacrifices and processions, might one see their kinship with the Greeks, but also from the mocking and jeering. For after the armed choruses there marched in procession the choruses of satyr-players, representing the Greek sikinnis. Their equipment, for those likened to Sileni, was woolly tunics, which some call "shaggy," and wraps of every flower; for those likened to Satyrs, girdles and goat-skins and upstanding manes of hair upon their heads and the like. These mocked and mimicked the earnest movements, transferring them to the more ridiculous.

The entries of triumphs too show the mocking and satyric sport to be ancient and native to the Romans. After these choruses there went by harpers in numbers and many flute-players; and after them those carrying the censers, on which spices and frankincense were burned the whole way, and those bearing the procession-vessels made of silver and gold, both the sacred and the public. Last of all there marched the images of the gods, borne on the shoulders of men, presenting forms like those fashioned among the Greeks, and equipment and symbols and gifts, of which each is handed down as the finder and giver to men—not only of Zeus and Hera and Athena and Poseidon and the others whom the Greeks reckon among the twelve gods, but also of the more ancient, from whom the twelve gods are fabled to have been born—Cronus and Rhea and Themis and Leto and the Fates and Mnemosyne and all the others to whom there are sacred rites and precincts among the Greeks; and of the later ones, fabled to have been born after Zeus took the rule—Persephone, Eileithyia, the Nymphs, the Muses, the Seasons, the Graces, Dionysus—and of as many demigods as, their souls having left their mortal bodies, are said to have gone up to heaven and obtained honours like the gods'—Heracles, Asclepius, the Dioscuri, Selene, Pan, and countless others.

And yet, if the founders of Rome and the establishers of this festival were barbarians, what fitted them to revere all the Greek gods and divinities, but to disregard their ancestral ones? The procession completed, the consuls and those of the priests whose office it was at once sacrificed oxen; and the manner of the sacrifices was the same as among us. For, having washed their hands and purified the victims with clean water and sprinkled the fruits of Demeter on their heads, then having prayed, they ordered the attendants to sacrifice them. Of these, some, while the victim still stood, struck its temples with a club; others, as it fell, put the slaughtering-knives beneath; and after this, having flayed and dismembered it, they took first-fruits from each entrail and every other limb, which, having moistened with spelt-meal, they offered on baskets to the sacrificers; and these, placing them on the altars, kindled them and poured wine over

the offerings as they were consecrated. That each thing was done by the laws established about sacrifice by the Greeks, it is easy to learn from the poetry of Homer. For he introduces the heroes washing their hands and using barley-meal, where he says: "Then they washed their hands and took up the barley-grains." And cutting the hair in three from the head and placing it on the fire, writing thus: "But he, taking first-fruits, cast the hairs of the head into the fire." And striking the foreheads of the victims with clubs and sacrificing them when fallen, as he does at the sacrifice of Eumaeus: "And he struck, taking first-fruits, with a billet of oak which he left when splitting. And the life left it; and they slaughtered and singed it."

And taking first-fruits from the entrails and from the other limbs, and moistening these with barley-meal and consecrating them on the altars, as he does at the same sacrifice: "And the swineherd laid the raw pieces, beginning from all the limbs, on the rich fat; and these he cast on the fire, having sprinkled them with barley-grits."

These things, which I have seen the Romans still doing in my time at the sacrifices, I know; and content with this one proof, I am persuaded that the founders of Rome were not barbarians, but Greeks gathered from many places. And kindred to these things did those suffer who, turned to spoils and plunder, were deprived of withdrawing in order and array; for these too, caught by the enemy, some were slaughtered, others taken prisoners. And it seemed to help toward their not being utterly destroyed that a great storm broke from heaven and a darkness, such as comes in deep mists, which gave the enemy hesitation about pursuing further, being unable to see far off.

Thrust away from this hope too, the king flees with a few to the city of the Gabini, of which he had appointed king the elder of his sons, Sextus, as I said before — being now grey in age, but having held the kingship twenty-five years. And Herminius and Horatius, having established a truce of the war with the Ardeates for fifteen years, led off the forces homeward. The royal constitution, then, having lasted, after the founding of Rome, two hundred and forty-four years in number, and having, under the last king, become a tyranny, was, for these causes and by these men, dissolved.

On the following night the consul, setting the army in motion, led it off in silence and in order, taking forethought to escape the enemy's notice; and he encamped beside a city called Longula about late evening, having chosen a hill sufficient to keep off assailants. There, waiting, he recovered with treatment those weakened by wounds, and consoled and took up those distressed at the unexpected disgrace of the calamity.
"A city is somehow like a human body. For each is compounded and made of many parts; and neither part has the same power as the parts within them, nor furnishes equal services.

The Romans, then, were in this state; but the Volscians, when day came and they learned that the enemy had abandoned the camp, advancing, encamped. Having stripped the enemy's dead and taken up the half-dead, for whom there was hope of safety, and made burial of their own dead, they removed to the nearest city, Antium; where, singing the paean for the victory and sacrificing in all the temples, they turned in the following days to revelries and pleasures.

"If, then, the parts of the human body should take each a separate sense and voice of their own, and then strife should fall among them, all the rest becoming of one mind against the belly alone, and the feet should say that the whole body rests upon them; the hands, that they work the crafts and procure the necessaries and fight enemies and furnish many other benefits to the common good; the shoulders, that all the burdens are carried upon them; the mouth, that it speaks; the head, that it sees and hears and, embracing all the other senses, holds them, through which the creature is preserved; and then they should say to the belly: 'But you, good lady, what of these do you do, or what is your favour and benefit to us? Nay, you are so far from doing and helping us accomplish anything of common use, that you even work against us and trouble us, and—a thing unbearable—compel us to serve you and to fetch from every quarter for the filling of your own desires.

Had they, then, remained at the victory then and wrought nothing further, the contest would have had a fair end for them. For the Romans would no longer have endured to come forth from the camp for war, but would have been content if they got away from the enemy's land, reckoning inglorious flight better than manifest death. But as it was, reaching after more, they cast away the glory from the former victory too.

"'Come, why do we not lay claim to freedom and rid ourselves of the many businesses we endure for her sake?' One could not say otherwise.

For hearing from scouts and from those who had run away from the camp that the Romans saved were quite few, and of these the most wounded, they conceived much contempt of them, and at once, snatching up their arms, ran against them. "In the same way conceive also concerning a city. "'a leader?' Learning, then, commoners, that just as in our bodies the belly, ill-reviled by the many, nourishes the body while it is nourished and preserves it while it is preserved, and is a kind of common feast distributing to all what is fitting and the cause of the harmony, so in cities the council, which administers the common affairs and provides for what befits each, preserves and guards and sets right everything—cease your envious cries against it, that you were cast from your country and that as wanderers and beggars you go about because of it. These, making their march for the most part secretly through mountains and by night, entered the camp unobserved by the enemy. Aemilius, then, had become bolder at the arrival of the allies; and the enemy, vainly trusting in their numbers and lifted up by the Romans' not coming out to battle, mounted the hill, having densened their companies; and the Romans, letting them mount at leisure and toil much about the palisade, when the signals of battle were raised, tearing apart the camp at many points, fall upon them; and some, coming to close quarters, fought with their swords, while others from the strongholds pelted the assailants with stones and javelins and lances, and no missile was without aim, many being packed in a small space.

The Volscians, then, are dislodged from the hill, having lost many of their own, and, taking to flight, with difficulty get safe to their own camp. The Romans, as being now in safety, came down to their fields, from which they took provisions and the other things of which there was scarcity in the camp.

And, having made a decree of the senate, they proclaimed a day on which those of military age must present themselves. After this there was much tumult through the city, and seditious speeches of the poorest, who thought fit neither to obey the decrees of the senate nor to be subject to the power of the consuls, because they had falsified the promises about the land-distribution to them; and, gathering in a body against the tribunes, they reproached them with treachery and cried out, invoking their alliance.

To the others, then, it did not seem a fitting time, a foreign war being on foot, to rekindle the civic enmities; but one of them, Gaius Maenius, said he would not betray the commoners, nor permit the consuls to enrol an army, unless they should first appoint the men to bound the public land and write and bring out before the people the decree about the distribution. The consuls opposing this and making the war in hand a pretext for conceding him nothing of what he asked, he said he would give them no heed, but

would hinder the levy with all his power. And he did this; yet he did not prevail to the end. For the consuls, coming forth outside the city into the adjoining plain, set up the general's chairs; there they made the military levy, and those who would not obey the laws, since they were unable to lead them off, they punished in money—those who had farms, cutting these down and demolishing their steadings; and those whose livelihood was farming on others' possessions, carrying off and driving away the ox-teams and cattle and beasts of burden prepared for the work and all manner of implements by which the land is worked and the crops gathered.

And the tribune hindering the levy was no longer able to do anything. For those holding the tribunician power are masters of nothing outside the city; for their power is circumscribed by the walls, and it is not lawful for them even to spend a night away from the city, save for one occasion, on which all the magistrates of the city, going up to the Alban Mount, perform a common sacrifice to Jupiter on behalf of the Latin nation.

This custom remains to our times, that the tribunes are masters of nothing outside the city; and indeed of the civil war of the Romans in my own age, which was the greatest of the wars before it, the moving pretext—seeming, among many others, to be the greater and alone sufficient to divide the city—was this: that certain of the tribunes, charging that they had been driven from the city by force by the one then holding the affairs in Italy, that they might be masters of nothing, fled for refuge, as having nowhere to turn, to the one holding the armies in Gaul.

And he, using this pretext, as one piously and justly aiding a most sacred magistracy of the people deprived of its power against the oaths of the forefathers, himself came with arms into the city and restored the men to their office.

The people, when they heard this, with a great cry that held a long while both praised the man and urged the envoys to grant them this also. Then, indeed, the commoners, enjoying nothing of the tribunician power, gave up their boldness and, coming to those appointed over the levy, swore the sacred oath and were enrolled under the standards.
