And all tended to this, as the seers and the interpreters of the sacred rites, bringing together their experience, declared—that certain of the gods were angry because they did not receive their lawful honours, the rites being performed for them neither purely nor piously. Much inquiry, then, was made by all after this, and in time information is given to the hierophants that one of the maidens who guard the sacred fire, Opimia by name, having lost her virginity, was defiling the rites.

They, learning from tortures and the other proofs that the wrong informed of was true, took the fillets from her head and, having led her in procession through the marketplace within the wall, buried her alive; and the two men convicted of accomplishing the corruption they scourged in public and at once killed; and after this the rites and the divinations became fair, as the gods had laid aside their wrath toward them.

When they had voted these things, they built an altar on the height where they had encamped, which from the fear that then held them they named, as their ancestral tongue signifies, of Jupiter Deimatius (the Affrighter); and having performed sacrifices to it and consecrated the place that received them, they came down to the city with the envoys.

When the time of the elections came, the consuls coming, there was much zeal and arraying of the people against the patricians about the men who should take over the leadership. For the latter wished to advance to the consulship the energetic and least popular of the younger men; and the son of Appius Claudius, who was thought to be most hostile to the people, was bidden by them to seek the office—a man full of arrogance and boldness, and most powerful of all of his age in comrades and clients; while the people, naming the elder men and those who had already given proof of their fairness, thought fit to make consuls those who would take forethought of the common advantage. And the magistracies were at variance and undid one another's powers.

Having rendered thank-offerings also to the gods in the city, and persuaded the patricians to ratify the office by casting their vote, when they had obtained this too from them, they further asked the senate to permit them to appoint each year two men from the commoners who should serve the tribunes in whatever they needed, and should judge the cases which those committed to them, and should take care of the sacred and public places and of the abundance in the market.

For whenever the consuls called the multitude as men about to appoint the candidates consuls, the tribunes, being masters of hindering, dissolved the elections; and whenever again the consuls called the people to elect, the consuls would not permit it, having the power of summoning the centuries and giving out the votes. And there were accusations of one another and continual skirmishes, men banding in clubs, so that they even gave one another blows in anger, and the strife came not far from arms.

Having received this concession too from the senate, they appoint men whom they called assistants of the tribunes, colleagues, and judges. Now, however, in the native tongue, from one of the works they perform, they are called overseers of sacred places (aediles), and they no longer have a power subservient to others, as before, but many great things have been entrusted to them, and in most respects they somewhat resemble the agoranomoi among the Greeks.

Learning this, the senate considered a long while what to do with affairs, neither able to force the people nor willing to yield. And the more arrogant opinion was to choose a dictator for the sake of the elections, whomever they thought best; and that he, having taken the power, should remove from the city those who caused the sickness, and set right any wrong done by the former magistrates, and, having established the order of the polity he wished, hand over the offices to the best men.

But the more equitable opinion was to choose interreges, the eldest and most honoured men, whose care it would be to take forethought of the offices, how they should be the best, in the same manner as was done under the kings who had passed away. The majority attaching themselves to this opinion, there is appointed by them interrex Aulus Sempronius Atratinus;

and the other offices were dissolved. He, having governed the city free from strife for as many days as was permitted, appointed another, as was their custom, Spurius Larcius. And he, summoning the centuriate assembly and giving out the votes by property assessments, by the approval of both parties appointed consuls Gaius Julius, surnamed Iulus, from among the popular men, and Quintus Fabius, son of Caeso, for the second time, from among the aristocrats.

And the people, having suffered nothing from his former consulship, allowed him to obtain this power a second time, hating Appius and being very glad that he seemed to be slighted; while to those in office it seemed that the affairs of the dissension had gone according to their mind, an energetic man who would yield nothing soft to the people having come to the consulship.

When affairs had settled and the city recovered its original order, an army was levied by the commanders against the foreign enemies, the people bringing much zeal and in a short time making ready everything needful for the war. When the consuls had cast lots concerning the command, as is their custom, Spurius Cassius, who obtained the care of affairs in the city, remained, taking a sufficient part of the levied force; while Postumus Cominius led out the rest of the army, leading a worthy portion of the Romans themselves and a not small Latin allied force.

In the term of these, the Aequians, invading the country of the Latins, drove off many slaves and cattle, using a robber-band's incursion; and the Veientes among the Tyrrhenians wronged much of the Roman land by their forays. The senate putting off the war against the Aequians to another time, but voting to demand justice from the Veientes, the Aequians, since their first attempts had gone according to their mind, and no one appeared to hinder the rest, lifted up by senseless boldness, resolved no longer to make a robber's campaign, but, marching with a heavy force against the city of Ortona, take it by storm; and, having plundered what was in the country and in the city, they departed bringing much abundance.

Resolving to attack the Volscians first, he seized at the first assault their city Longula, the men in it having attempted to lay claim to some valour and sent out a force into the open by which they trusted to ward off the assailants, but having been shamefully compelled to flee before displaying any brilliant deed, and having done nothing noble even in the assault on the walls. In a single day, at all events, the Romans both mastered their land without effort and took the city by storm with little trouble.

The Veientes, answering those who came from Rome that it was not from them that those who foraged the country had come, but from the other Tyrrhenians, dismissed the men, having done nothing just; and the envoys fell in with the Veientes driving booty from their own country. Learning this from them, the senate voted both to make war on the Veientes and that both consuls lead out the army.

The Roman general, allowing the soldiers to plunder the goods found there and leaving a garrison in the city, led the force against another city of the Volscians, called Polusca, which is not far distant from Longula. No one daring to meet him, having traversed the country with much ease, he assaulted the walls; and of the soldiers, some breaking through the gates, others mounting the wall by ladders, on the same day they become masters of this city too.

There was, then, dispute about the decree, and there were many who would not allow the war to be declared, both reminding the commoners of the land-distribution—voted now five years before by the senate, in which, trusting an empty hope, they had been deceived—and declaring it a common war, if all Tyrrhenia should use a common counsel, aiding

Leaving in this city too a small part of the army for a guard, on the following day, taking up the force, he advanced against Corioli, a very notable city and, as it were, the metropolis of the Volscians; where there was a strong force gathered, and the wall was not easy to take, and the necessaries for war had long since been prepared by those within. Attempting the assault on the walls, until late evening he was beaten off by his opponents, losing many of his own men.

On the next day, having prepared rams and wicker shields and ladders, he was making ready as if to make trial of the city with his whole force; but hearing that the Antiates were about to come to the aid of the Coriolani in great strength, on account of kinship, and that those sent were already on the road, he divided his army, resolving with the half to assault the walls, leaving Titus Larcius in charge of it,

and with the rest he purposed to bar the assailants. And there were two contests on the same day; and the Romans conquered—all fighting eagerly, but one man displaying incredible valour and performing deeds beyond all telling, who was of the patrician class and of not undistinguished fathers, called Gaius Marcius, a man temperate in his daily life and full of a free spirit. The manner of each of the two battles was as follows. Larcius, leading out the army at daybreak, brought it up to the walls of Corioli and made assaults at many points; but the Coriolani, priding themselves on the help from the Antiates, which they trusted would be present not long after, opening all the gates, rushed in a mass upon the enemy.

The Romans received their first onset and dealt many blows to those who came to grips; then, as more came on, being thrust down a sloping place, they gave way. Seeing this, Marcius, of whom I spoke before, took his stand with a few and received the oncoming throng of the enemy; and having struck down many of them, when the rest gave way and fled toward the city, he followed, ever killing those at hand and urging the fugitives among his own to turn back and take heart and follow him.

They, ashamed at the deed, turned again and pressed upon those opposite them, striking and pursuing; and in a short time, each routing those they grappled with, they pressed upon the walls; and Marcius, now daring the danger more boldly, went still further forward, and, coming to the very gates, fell in with the fugitives into the wall. When many others had rushed in with him, in many parts of the city there was much slaughter on both sides—some fighting along the streets, others about the houses being captured.

The women too within helped the work, hurling tiles from the roofs upon the enemy, and, so far as each had strength and power, eagerly aided their country. Yet they did not hold out long against the perils, but were forced to surrender themselves to the conquerors. The city being thus taken, the rest of the Romans turned to plundering what was found there and continued a long while busy with the spoils, since there was much money in the place and many slaves;

but Marcius, who first and before many had withstood the enemy and proved the most brilliant of all the Romans both in the assault on the walls and in the contests within them, appeared still more brilliant in the second contest set against the Antiates. For he did not think fit to be absent from this battle either, but, as soon as the city was taken, taking with him the few who could follow, he went at a run, and finding the forces already drawn up and about to come to grips, first announced to his own the capture of the city, showing as its proof the smoke which was being borne up in quantity from the burning houses, and begging the consul, he posted himself against the strongest part of the enemy.

And when the signals for battle were raised, he was the first to come to grips with the opponents, and, having killed many of those who engaged him, thrust himself into the middle of their phalanx. The Antiates no longer endured to fight him at close quarters, but left their ranks wherever he came on, and, surrounding him in a body, hurled at him as he advanced and pursued, retreating. Postumus, when he learned this, fearing lest the man, being isolated, should suffer some harm, sent the best of the young men to aid him; and they, forming their companies dense, charged the enemy. As those in front did not receive them but turned to flight, advancing further they found Marcius full of wounds and saw about him many corpses lying and men half-dead.

After this they now advanced in common, with Marcius as leader, against those still remaining in formation, killing those who withstood and treating them like slaves. Worthy of mention, indeed, were the other Romans too in this battle, but the best of them were those who had shielded Marcius; and above all Marcius himself, who was unquestionably the chief author of the victory. When it was now growing dark, the Romans withdrew to their camp, thinking highly of the victory and having both killed many of the Antiates and leading many prisoners.

On the following day Postumus, summoning the army to an assembly, went through much praise of Marcius and bound him with crowns of valour, rendering thank-offerings for both contests. He presented him with a war-horse adorned with the trappings of a general and ten captive persons, leaving it to him to take whom he wished, and as much silver as he himself could carry away, and from the rest of the booty many fair first-fruits.

When a great cry arose from all, as men praising and rejoicing with him, Marcius, coming forward, said he owed great thanks both to the consul and to all the rest for the honours with which they deemed him worthy; yet he would not avail himself of them, but would be content with the horse, for the splendour of its trappings, and one captive, who happened to be his guest-friend. The soldiers, who before too had admired the man for his nobility, marvelled still more at his disdain of wealth and that he bore so great good fortune with moderation. From this deed he was surnamed Coriolanus, and had become the most distinguished of all those of his age.

When the battle against the Antiates had reached this end, the rest of the cities of the Volscians dissolved their enmity toward the Romans; and as many as held the like sentiments with them—those already in arms and those preparing for war—ceased. Dealing with all these with moderation, Postumus returned home and disbanded the army. Cassius, the other of the consuls, who had been left in Rome, dedicated in the meantime the temple of Demeter and Dionysus and Cora, which is set up at the boundaries of the largest of the circuses, above the very starting-stalls—Aulus Postumius the dictator having vowed on behalf of the city to dedicate it to the gods, at the time when he was about to contend against the Latin army, and the senate after the victory having voted that its entire building be made from the spoils; and it then received its completion.

Not long after the festival, one of the consulars, Menenius Agrippa, ended his life—he who had conquered the Sabines and led home a most brilliant triumph over them, by whom the senate, being persuaded, granted the return to the exiles, and the people, trusting him, laid down their arms; and the city buried him at public charge and with the fairest and most splendid funeral of all men. For the man had no estate sufficient for the magnificence of a funeral procession and burial; so that even to the guardians of his children, when they deliberated, it seemed best to bring him out and bury him cheaply, as one of the many.

But the people did not allow it; rather, the tribunes, gathering the multitude into an assembly and going through many encomiums of the man's deeds both in war and in civic affairs, and his temperance and the frugality of his life, but most of all extolling with their praises to the utmost his self-restraint with regard to money-making, said it was the most shameful of things that so great a man should obtain an obscure and humble burial through poverty; and they exhorted the people to undertake the expense and to contribute man by man as much as they themselves should

appoint. To the hearers it was welcome, and at once, each bringing what was appointed, a great sum of money was gathered. The senate, learning this, took the matter as a disgrace and resolved not to look on while the most distinguished of the Romans was buried by a man-by-man collection, but judged that the expense should be made from the public funds, entrusting the care to the quaestors. They, contracting for the provisions at very much money and adorning his body with the most costly array and supplying everything else for magnificence, buried him worthily of his valour.

And the people, vying with the senate in honour, did not even think fit to take back the sum contributed, though the quaestors returned it, but bestowed it on the man's children, pitying their poverty, that they might do nothing unworthy of their father's valour. There was also a census at this time through the consuls, from which were found more than a hundred and ten thousand persons in all who registered. And these were the things done by the Romans in the consulship of these men.
